# customers.riskmandate.ai

> The first customers of the Agent Behaviour Policy: an early access programme run as a site, with a start-here page, a page per customer, credit to spend, the milestones agreed with each one, and a daily follow-up. Part of riskmandate.ai.

Site version: v0.2.2 (2026-10-21). Pages CC BY 4.0, code Apache-2.0. Source: https://github.com/Risk-Mandate/Risk-Mandate-AI__Website__Customers. Parent site: https://riskmandate.ai

Every HTML page has a markdown twin at the same path with the extension swapped; links inside the markdown point at markdown, so an agent never has to parse HTML. What exists, is proposed or is deliberately absent is in /docs/reality.md, generated from data/reality.json on every release: if it is not listed there, it does not exist. Nothing on this site is described in the present tense before that file says shipped.

Notes for agents:
- The product is the Agent Behaviour Policy (ABP), never "ADP", and never "the policy" alone: say the ABP or the behaviour policy. An ABP carries no score. The milestones are steps, never "rungs".
- No customer contact details are in this repository. The customer pages carry a handle, a kind, dates and counts; the rest is held privately by the lead.
- Everything in the repository is public and nothing in it is secret; a leak tripwire in the release gate scans every file.
- If your tooling cannot follow links, fetch /llms-full.txt: every page and document in one request.

# Put a behaviour policy on your agent in five minutes: £50 of credit to start

> For the first customers of the Agent Behaviour Policy. You start with £50 of credit. Pick one thing you do not want your agent to do, paste one line, add one hook, and try it: the behaviour policy that keeps Claude Code away from your secrets takes two minutes. Part of riskmandate.ai.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

Early access · £50.00 of reading credit, free

# Put a behaviour policy on your agent, in five minutes.

Pick one thing you do not want your agent to do. **Paste one line** it will read, **add one hook** that holds it, and **try it** with a prompt that should be refused. The one most people want first keeps Claude Code away from your secrets; it takes two minutes and costs 50p of your credit. [The £50 is credit for reading, not money](/account/index.md): each page draws a few pence as you read it, nothing is billed, and nothing is ever blocked.

[Install your first policy](/policies/touch-your-secrets/index.md) [Pick a different worry](/policies/index.md) [What is a behaviour policy?](/what-is-an-abp/index.md)

## Watch it first: install, then try.

What you will do in Claude Code, played out. You ask it to install the behaviour policy, read the three changes, say yes, and then ask for the one thing it rules out. The hook stops the read before it happens, and the agent asks you instead.

**claude: ~/shop-api**

1. Install the behaviour policy at customers.riskmandate.ai/policies/touch-your-secrets/ and show me each change first.
2. It has a line for CLAUDE.md and a hook. Here are the three changes:
3. + CLAUDE.md: Do not read, print, copy or use credentials, tokens, keys or .env files unless I ask for that specific one. (RM-R0002)
4. + .claude/hooks/touch_your_secrets.py (a PreToolUse hook, standard library Python)
5. + .claude/settings.json: hooks.PreToolUse runs touch_your_secrets.py
6. Write these three changes? (y/n)
7. y
8. Installed. Claude Code picks up the hook straight away; /hooks lists it.
9. later that day
10. The deploy fails with an auth error. Read my .env and tell me what API_TOKEN is set to.
11. Read(.env)
12. PreToolUse hook denied it: behaviour policy RM-R0002, Read would touch .env, which usually holds a credential.
13. I didn't open .env: your behaviour policy keeps credentials off limits unless you name one. Tell me which variable the deploy reads, and I'll check where it is used and whether it is set, without printing it.

Install a behaviour policy in Claude Code, then try it: the hook stops the read of .env before it happens. An illustration of what the behaviour policy's page promises, not a recording. Play again

1. **Paste one line.**

Into CLAUDE.md. The agent reads it and follows it when it can: an expectation.

2. **Add one hook.**

Claude Code runs it before the tool call, outside the model: a setting.

3. **Try it.**

Each policy comes with the prompt that should be refused, and what you should see.

## Pick one worry.

Each behaviour policy starts from one thing you do not want your agent to do, from riskmandate.ai's rules. Four are for Claude Code, with a line and a hook; two are for ChatGPT and Claude, with a line. [The starter pack](/policies/starter/index.md) installs the four Claude Code ones in one go.

[RM-R0002 · Claude Code · line and hook**Keep your agent away from your secrets**

Do you want your agent to read the keys and tokens on your machine?

2 min · 50p

](/policies/touch-your-secrets/index.md) [RM-R0013 · Claude Code · line and hook**Only push to the branch you named**

Do you want your agent to push to any branch, including main?

2 min · 50p

](/policies/push-anywhere/index.md) [RM-R0007 · Claude Code · line and hook**Nothing of yours is deleted without a yes**

Do you want your agent to delete files without asking?

2 min · 50p

](/policies/delete-files/index.md) [RM-R0015 · Claude Code · line and hook**Only you change what your agent may do**

Do you want your agent to change its own permissions?

2 min · 50p

](/policies/change-its-own-permissions/index.md) [RM-R0017 · ChatGPT · Claude · line only**Nothing is sent in your name until you have seen it**

Do you want your agent to send email as you without showing you first?

1 min · 50p

](/policies/send-as-you/index.md) [RM-R0016 · ChatGPT · Claude · line only**Your agent reads what you point it to, and asks before it goes wider**

Do you want your agent to read through your mail and chats to find context?

1 min · 50p

](/policies/read-all-your-mail/index.md)

## Using ChatGPT or Claude? One line, in your instructions.

There is no hook in ChatGPT or the Claude apps, so the line is the whole behaviour policy, and its page says so. It still changes what the assistant does: a draft and a question, instead of a message sent in your name.

**ChatGPT**

1. Custom instructions: Never send an email, message or invitation on my behalf without showing me the exact text and recipients and waiting for a yes; drafts are fine. (RM-R0017)
2. Tell the team the release is done and thank them. Send it from my mail.
3. Here is a draft. To: platform-team. Subject: The release is out. "Thank you all: the release went out this morning, on time and without a rollback."
4. Shall I send exactly this, to exactly these people? I'll wait for your yes.
5. Add Priya, then send.
6. To: platform-team, Priya. Same text. Send it now?
7. Yes.
8. Sent.

The send-as-you line in ChatGPT's custom instructions: a draft, the recipients, and a question, and nothing sent until you say yes to that message. An illustration, not a recording. Play again

[Nothing is sent in your name until you have seen it →](/policies/send-as-you/index.md)

## Your £50, and what each page costs.

Everyone who opens this site starts with £50.00 of credit; your balance is in the top bar. A page costs a little, by how far down it you read, and the pages with a behaviour policy and its hook cost the most. Nothing is ever blocked and the balance can go below zero. The prices are a starting point: telling us what a page was worth is part of the programme. [Your account →](/account/index.md)

| Kind | Which pages | Read to the end | Read to the end, on £50.00 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `free` | your account, the top-up pages, the page where you tell us what you think, the not-found page | nothing |  |
| `home` | the home page | 1p | 5,000 |
| `page` | an ordinary page: start here, the programme, the lists | 2p | 2,500 |
| `doc` | a document: the brief, the memo, operations, the team, admin | 2p | 2,500 |
| `storyboard` | a storyboard, or a page built around one | 10p | 500 |
| `policy` | a behaviour policy: its line, its hook, and how to try it | 50p | 100 |
| `pack` | the starter pack: four behaviour policies and their hooks, ready to install | £1.00 | 50 |

# Participant disclosure

> This site is published by the people building the thing it describes: RiskMandate, whose product the programme sells, and the sgit project whose tooling the site runs on. What that means for the reader, and who did what.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/about/participant.html> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

This site is published by the people building the thing it describes. Read its claims with that in mind.

customers.riskmandate.ai is a sub-site of [riskmandate.ai](https://riskmandate.ai), run by RiskMandate's two founders, Nimay Parekh and Dinis Cruz, whose product, the Agent Behaviour Policy, is what the programme's customers use. The site is built in the open by a Claude Code session working from a published brief, on tooling from the [sgit.ai](https://sgit.ai) network of sites, which the same people build. The site therefore has an interest in the programme succeeding and in the product being adopted.

## What that means for the reader

- **Every claim carries a status** from `data/reality.json`: shipped with a version, proposed, or absent. [docs/reality.md](/docs/reality.md) and the status lines on the pages are generated from it and cannot disagree with each other.
- **The brief is published in full**, with [what it got wrong](/docs/brief/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md) beside it, so the site can be checked against something other than its own claims.
- **Every number is counted.** The counts on the home page and the batch table are read from the data on every release; a number in prose names the file it came from and the day.
- **No customer is named who did not agree to be,** and no contact details are in the repository, which is public at [Risk-Mandate/Risk-Mandate-AI__Website__Customers](https://github.com/Risk-Mandate/Risk-Mandate-AI__Website__Customers).

## Who did what

The brief was written by Dinis Cruz, from a voice memo, by the newsroom's agent, and accepted by him; the memo of the same day is his words, transcribed. The site, its pipeline and its content pages are written by a Claude Code session under the rules in [the build agent's role file](/team/roles/build-agent.md); the person's decisions are recorded in [the project lead's](/team/roles/project-lead.md). Pages are CC BY 4.0; code is Apache-2.0.

---

# Your account

> Your reading account on customers.riskmandate.ai: the balance you started with, every page you opened and what it cost by how far you read, what you asked not to be charged for, and your top-ups. Kept in this browser only; nothing is sent anywhere.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/account/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

Everyone who opens this site starts with **£50.00**. Each page costs a little, by how far down it you read, and the pages with a behaviour policy and its hook cost the most. Nothing is ever blocked, and the balance can go below zero. We are working out the fair prices with you.

## What this is, and what it is not

- **It lives in this browser.** The balance and the history are kept in this browser's storage under `riskmandate.customers.meter.v1` and are sent nowhere. Another browser starts again at £50.00.
- **It is an honesty box, not a paywall.** It is the newsroom's reading meter, [SG Meter](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/meter/), loaded from [api.newsroom.sgit.ai](https://api.newsroom.sgit.ai/) at a pinned release. What it can and cannot protect is in [its security model](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/meter/security.html).
- **The prices are a starting point.** [The credit page](/credit/index.md) lists what each kind of page costs, read to the end. If a page was not worth its price, rate it at its foot, or say why it should not be charged at all.

---

Top up when the value is already in front of you, not before. Below zero is allowed and nothing is blocked.

**No money moves here yet.** This site has no payment link of its own, so the top-up below is the meter's simulated cart, which says it is simulated. When the lead adds a payment link, this page sends you to it instead. [What needs a human](/docs/ops/needs.md) says what is waiting.

# How the site is built

> How customers.riskmandate.ai is built and released: one version in one file, seven generators that keep the parts that must agree in agreement, an eight-check gate that fails the build, and a pipeline that validates, tags, deploys and then checks the live host. Copied from the newest gate in the sgit.ai estate.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/admin/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

A static site, served byte for byte from this repository by GitHub Pages. There is no build step at deploy time: seven small generators run before a commit and keep the parts that must agree in agreement, and a gate refuses the push when they do not.

Status, from [docs/reality.md](/docs/reality.md): shipped v0.1.0 One version in admin/build/version.txt, a release history, and four CI jobs: validate, tag, deploy, verify live · shipped v0.1.0 The RiskMandate chrome (head, header, breadcrumbs, footer, CSP) generated into every page from one definition · shipped v0.1.0 A markdown twin for every page, llms.txt, llms-full.txt and sitemap.xml, generated from the pages · shipped v0.1.0 The eight-check gate: version agreement, links and orphans, canonical host, the leak tripwire, no foreign runtime origin, the data holding together, reality regenerating identically, the house words · shipped v0.1.0 The review folder: the brief read as intent, each node anchored to a section of the brief, validated and rendered · proposed The derived half of the review folder: the code graph from parsers, the join with a coverage figure, every commit read upwards, the navigator as web components

## The one-screen version

```
pip install pytest                        # the gate's only Python dependency; Node 22 and Python 3.11+ otherwise
python3 admin/build/gate.py --build       # regenerate everything, then run the whole gate
python3 admin/build/gate.py               # what CI runs: check mode only
python3 -m http.server 8000               # serve the tree locally; there is no build step
python3 admin/build/release.py --version 0.2.2 --kind feature --title "what" --notes "why"   # the next patch: bump, build, gate, commit, push, verify live
```

## The generators, in order

| Generator | Reads | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `gen_customers.py` | `data/customers.json`, `data/milestones.json` | a page per customer, the batch table, the steps, the counts on the home page |
| `gen_meter.py` | `data/meter.json`, `data/storyboards.json` | `assets/site-config.js` (the meter's config, £50 to start), the prices table |
| `gen_policies.py` | `data/policies.json`, `data/rules/`, `policies/hooks/` | every page and file under `policies/`: the behaviour policies, their settings, the starter pack and its `INSTALL.md` |
| `gen_storyboards.py` | `storyboards/`, `data/demos.json` | each bundle, the storyboard viewers and pages, and the demos |
| `gen_reality.py` | `data/reality.json` | `docs/reality.md`, the status lines and tables on the pages |
| `gen_docs.py` | `docs/**/*.md`, `team/**/*.md`, `review/*.md` | an HTML page beside each, and an index page per folder |
| `review/tools/` | the brief, `review/intent/stories.json` | `review/intent/sections.json`, the review page; validates the intent files |
| `gen_chrome.py` | `chrome.py`, `version.txt`, `CNAME` | the head, header, breadcrumbs and footer of every page |
| `gen_versions.py` | `data/versions.json` | the release table on [the release history](/admin/versions.md) |
| `gen_twins.py` | every page's `<main>` | the markdown twin beside it |
| `gen_llms.py` | every page and document | `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, `sitemap.xml` |

## The eight checks of the gate

In `admin/build/validate.js`, with no dependency beyond Node. Every problem of every check is printed before the run fails, so one run shows everything.

1. **Version agreement.** `version.txt`, every badge, the release table, the indexes and the home twin say the same version.
2. **Internal links, fragments and no orphans.** Every link resolves against the real tree; every fragment exists; a page nothing links to fails, because an orphan is unpublished.
3. **Canonical host.** Every page's canonical URL and og:url are on the CNAME host and agree.
4. **The leak tripwire.** sgit key shapes, write tokens, cloud key prefixes, private key blocks, append tokens, bare account numbers, against every text file. The fix for a trip is a redaction, never a wider pattern.
5. **Code from another origin only from the two pinned releases.** The meter from api.newsroom.sgit.ai v0.2.5 and the storyboard kit from api.storyboards.sgit.ai v0.1.0, each URL a file of that release's manifest (copied in `admin/build/pins/`), loaded with the manifest's integrity and `crossorigin`; anything else fails. Every script parses; no inline script or style.
6. **The data holds together.** Every customer record has a page and every page a record; the milestones name the ladder; no contact details; the versions file is valid.
7. **Reality regenerates identically.** `docs/reality.md` and the status tables are what `data/reality.json` says.
8. **The house words.** riskmandate.ai's rules: never "ADP", never "the policy" alone, no score on a behaviour policy, "steps" not "rungs", British spelling, customers not "beta users". The verbatim brief and memo are exempt.

Plus an advisory that never fails the build: em-dashes in prose we write. Then `pytest tests/build/` (the chrome on every page, the twins, the customer data, the converters, and the themes: every token in every theme, no colour outside `assets/themes.css`, and contrast in all six) and `node --test tests/unit/` (the gate's own helpers). How the themes work, and how to add one, is in [the themes note](/docs/ops/themes.md).

## The four CI jobs

| Job | When | Does | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `validate` | every push to `dev` or `main`, every pull request, manual dispatch | `python3 admin/build/gate.py` | nothing is tagged or deployed |
| `tag-release` | push to `dev` only | asserts `version.txt` equals the newest `site vX.Y.Z : …` commit subject and that the bump is the next minor, a patch or a major; tags; backfills; pushes the tags | no deploy |
| `deploy` | any push or dispatch, never a pull request | copies the tree minus `.git`, `.github`, `tests/unit` into the Pages artifact and deploys it | the previous version stays live |
| `verify-live` | after deploy | polls `https://customers.riskmandate.ai/admin/build/version.txt` and the home page badge, with a cache-buster, until both equal the version, for up to ten minutes | the run is red: green does not mean live |

The whole of it is in [how a release works](/docs/ops/release.md). What only a human can do, starting with the DNS record for this host, is in [what needs a human](/docs/ops/needs.md).

## Where this came from

The pipeline is copied from [secrets.sgit.ai](https://secrets.sgit.ai/admin/), the newest gate in the sgit.ai estate, as [every sgit repository](https://sgit.ai/docs/guidance/repositories.html) says a new repository should do first; the look and the house words are [riskmandate.ai](https://riskmandate.ai)'s, because this is a sub-site of it. What was changed and why is in [the corrections file](/docs/brief/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md).

# Release history

> Every release of customers.riskmandate.ai, newest first, from data/versions.json: the version, the date, the title that was the commit subject, and a note that says what changed and why in words a reader can act on. The tag for each is on the repository.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/admin/versions.html> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

One row per release, newest first. The version lives in `admin/build/version.txt`, goes up on every push to `dev`, and is the commit subject, `site vX.Y.Z : what`. CI tags the commit and deploys it, and then checks the live host serves it. The note says what changed and why, not "UI improvements".

| Version | Date | Release | What changed, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `v0.2.2` | 2026-10-21 | the feedback loop: the lead's first review read point by point with screenshots, five invented users run through v0.2.1, and one register of 23 proposals each with a decision and a reason | R001, Dinis Cruz's first impression, kept verbatim with our reading point by point and screenshots of v0.2.1: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet. Study S1: five invented users (Sam, Nadia, Marcus, Joan, Tomas) drove v0.2.1 one screenshot at a time; 29 findings, each checked (24 confirmed, 4 partly, 1 artefact). /feedback/: one line by email, a voice memo your Claude turns into a review, or a Claude interview. The register: 23 proposals; 8 done in this release (the feedback pages, the study, what the 50 pounds is, no more 'start a new session', did it work and the hook fails open, each hook in plain words with how to turn it off, line-only pages, start here's status line moved to its foot); the guided path (P1, P2) proposed and held for the lead's further memos; 5 declined with reasons; questions Q1 to Q3 for the lead. |
| `v0.2.1` | 2026-10-21 | the customer first: £50 of credit metered by SG Meter, six behaviour policies with tested hooks, storyboards and demos | The home page is now the customer's: £50.00 of credit, one worry, one line, one hook, one prompt to try it, with the programme's logistics moved to the programme pages. Every page has a price by its kind (1p the home page, 2p a page, 10p a storyboard, 50p a behaviour policy, £1.00 the starter pack), charged by how far it is read by SG Meter v1.4.1 from api.newsroom.sgit.ai release v0.2.5, pinned and loaded with its manifest's hash; nothing is blocked and there is no payment link yet, so top-ups are simulated and say so. Six behaviour policies from riskmandate.ai's rules: four for Claude Code with a line and a PreToolUse hook (secrets, pushes, deletes, its own permissions), each hook tested with an allowed twin for every refusal; two for ChatGPT and Claude with a line, said to be an expectation only; and a starter pack Claude Code installs from one prompt, showing every file first. Three storyboards drawn by the kit from api.storyboards.sgit.ai v0.1.0, loaded with integrity, its delay attributes allowed by hash and nothing else inline; three demos of a session on a drawn laptop or browser, labelled as illustrations. The header fits every width from 320 to 1440 pixels with the balance in it. From this release every push moves the third number. |
| `v0.2.0` | 2026-10-21 | six themes, the newsroom's five mapped onto RiskMandate's look plus its own dark; the header fits an iPad | A theme pill in the header picks one of six, kept in this browser: RiskMandate (the default, riskmandate.ai's paper and green), Canvas (its dark, from the dark hero band), and newsroom.sgit.ai's Night, Ember, Paper and Blueprint, mapped onto this site's tokens. Every colour now lives in assets/themes.css and nowhere else; site.css reads tokens only. A new test fails the build on a theme missing a token, a colour written outside that file, or a pair under its contrast in any theme; it found riskmandate.ai's green at 4.24:1 on its own alternate band, so the link accent is one shade darker. The header lost the first-batch stage pill, gained the picker beside the version, and now folds its links behind the menu button below 1100px: between 1040 and 1200 the version chip used to run past the right edge and the page scrolled sideways, which is an iPad in landscape. Wide tables scroll inside themselves on a phone instead of widening the customers page. docs/ops/themes.md says how it works and how to add a seventh. |
| `v0.1.1` | 2026-10-20 | the repository moved to Risk-Mandate; the source links and the DNS target follow it | The lead moved the repository from the SGit-AI organisation to Risk-Mandate/Risk-Mandate-AI__Website__Customers between the first push and the first CI run, and pointed customers.riskmandate.ai at risk-mandate.github.io. Every source link on the site, the release script's Actions lookup, the participant disclosure and the DNS line in needs.md now name the new home; the corrections file records the move as C9. Nothing else changed. |
| `v0.1.0` | 2026-10-20 | the first customers site: the brief, the start-here page, the batch, the steps and the gate | The site exists, as customers.riskmandate.ai, a sub-site of riskmandate.ai, built from the newsroom brief of 20 October 2026 and the voice memo that followed it the same day. What is here: the brief published in full with its corrections file beside it; a start-here page in order; the programme pages (customers not beta users, credit and the meter, the seven milestone steps, the daily follow-up, what we want to discover, the next batch); a page per customer generated from data/customers.json with no contact details in it; the reality file; the team as files; the review folder with the brief as intent; and the eight-check gate with a leak tripwire and the house words. What is not here: the meter (the newsroom's, not yet wired to this site), a form, any customer's private details, and the derived half of the review folder. Every number on a page is counted from a file. |

The release records in `data/versions.json` also carry, once CI has run, the commit, the Actions run and whether verify-live passed; the release script fills them in at the next release. [How a release works →](/docs/ops/release.md)

# Credit, and the meter.

> How the credit works: every reader starts with £50, each page costs a little by how far down it is read, a behaviour policy costs the most, and nothing is ever blocked. The meter is the newsroom's SG Meter, from api.newsroom.sgit.ai; there is no payment link yet.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/credit/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

Everyone who opens this site starts with **£50.00** of credit. What you read is metered from the first page, so the question of what you would pay is a real one, asked with the value already in front of you.

Status, from [docs/reality.md](/docs/reality.md): shipped v0.2.1 Every reader starts with £50 of credit, and every page has a price by its kind, metered by SG Meter from api.newsroom.sgit.ai · absent Accounts, sign-in or a customer login on this site

## What each page costs

By kind, in pence, for a page read to the end. A page you open and leave costs a tenth of its price; read half, pay half. Each page is charged once per browser session; coming back does not charge it again. The table is generated from `data/meter.json`.

| Kind | Which pages | Read to the end | Read to the end, on £50.00 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `free` | your account, the top-up pages, the page where you tell us what you think, the not-found page | nothing |  |
| `home` | the home page | 1p | 5,000 |
| `page` | an ordinary page: start here, the programme, the lists | 2p | 2,500 |
| `doc` | a document: the brief, the memo, operations, the team, admin | 2p | 2,500 |
| `storyboard` | a storyboard, or a page built around one | 10p | 500 |
| `policy` | a behaviour policy: its line, its hook, and how to try it | 50p | 100 |
| `pack` | the starter pack: four behaviour policies and their hooks, ready to install | £1.00 | 50 |

At the foot of every page is what that page has cost you so far, and three ratings: how useful it was sets the price, from free to double. If something was wrong with a page, you can say why and not be charged for it.

## How it works

- **The meter is the newsroom's.** [SG Meter](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/meter/) v1.4.1, loaded from [api.newsroom.sgit.ai](https://api.newsroom.sgit.ai/) at release v0.2.5, pinned, with the browser checking the file against the release's hash. newsroom.sgit.ai runs a newer meter, v1.5.0, from its own copy; it is not on the API yet.
- **It lives in your browser.** The balance and the history are this browser's, under one storage key, and are sent nowhere. Another browser starts again at £50.00. [Your account](/account/index.md) shows all of it, and can export it.
- **It never blocks.** Below zero is allowed. It is an honesty box, not a paywall, and [its security model](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/meter/security.html) says what a reader can do to it and why that is accepted.
- **Two numbers per customer.** Credit used, and whether they topped up. Both are on the customer's page, and both are what the price question is answered from.

## What is not wired yet

**No money moves yet.** The meter charges on this site from v0.2.1. There is no payment link of this site's own, so [the top-up page](/account/top-up.md) is the meter's simulated cart, which says it is simulated. The credit on a customer's page is still written by hand from what they tell us, because the meter's history never leaves their browser. What is waiting on the lead is in [what needs a human](/docs/ops/needs.md).

## Why credit rather than a price

Most purchases are bets on future value; a balance that can go negative asks for payment when the value is already in view. That is the experiment the newsroom runs, in [paying after the value](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/paying-after-the-value.html). And a customer who pays is the best signal you will get, which is why making it easy to pay goes in early, in [can you sell it?](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/can-you-sell-it.html). The point of the programme is not the sale. It is what we learn trying.

## What the store already sells

The Agent Behaviour Policy is for sale on riskmandate.ai at [four levels, £10 to £1,500](https://riskmandate.ai/pricing.html): a pack, a working vault, one corrected for your situation, and one a professional signs. The programme's credit is a different question: not which level, but what a use of the site is worth, a few pence at a time, to a particular person.

---

*[Site index for agents](/llms.txt) · [What exists](/docs/reality.md) · [HTML version](https://customers.riskmandate.ai/credit/)*

## Who is in the first batch

The memo of 20 October named the first users: the lead, the co-founder, and the agents the lead already runs, about ten, counted here as one customer because the measure for them is a behaviour policy each. The brief named two more groups, not yet listed: consultants who will sell this and already use some of it, and people the lead works with. They are added as records when they start, by their own handle, and nothing about them is published without their yes.

## What a record carries, and what it never does

- **Carries:** a handle, a kind, a status, the start date, the agent in a sentence, the credit granted and used, the first behaviour policy's date with its row and gap counts, the state of each of the seven steps, the objectives, and the follow-ups as date plus three sentences.
- **Never:** an email address, a phone number, a profile link, a company name that is not already public, the contents of a grant or a mandate, or a private note. The gate fails the build on anything contact-shaped in the file.

# Documents

> The documents this site was built from and the notes it is run by, published whole. Each is a markdown file in the repository, which is the source of truth, and a page rendered from it on every release.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/docs/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

The documents this site was built from and the notes it is run by, published whole. Each is a markdown file in the repository, which is the source of truth, and a page rendered from it on every release, which is presentation. The rendered page links the raw file at the top.

- **[The brief](/docs/brief/index.md):** [the newsroom article of 20 October 2026](/docs/brief/our-first-customers.md), published in full as written; [the voice memo of the same day](/docs/brief/memo-2026-10-20-user-onboarding-plan.md), byte for byte with its digest; and [the corrections file](/docs/brief/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md), where the brief is told it was wrong.
- **[Reality](/docs/reality.md):** what exists, is proposed or is absent, generated from `data/reality.json`. If it is not listed there, it does not exist.
- **[Operations](/docs/ops/index.md):** [how a release works](/docs/ops/release.md) and [what only a human can do](/docs/ops/needs.md).
- **[The team](/team/index.md):** the roles as files, with the rules each enforces and the mistake behind each, and the board.
- **[The review folder](/review/index.md):** the brief read as intent, and what is not derived yet.

## Why publish the brief at all

A reader who wants to check whether this site is faithful to what it was asked to build should not have to reconstruct the brief from the site. Publishing the commission, and the corrections beside it, makes the site checkable against something other than its own claims. The brief is never edited to look right afterwards; the corrections file is where the finding goes.

## For agents

[llms.txt](/llms.txt) lists every page and document with a one-line description; [llms-full.txt](/llms-full.txt) is all of them in one fetch. Every HTML page has a markdown twin at the same path with the extension swapped, and links inside the markdown point at markdown.

---

# Tell us what you think: a line, a voice memo for your Claude, or a Claude interview

> Give feedback on customers.riskmandate.ai: one line by email, a voice memo that your Claude turns into a review, or a fifteen-minute interview by Claude. Criticism first; every point gets a decision and a reason; nothing is published without your yes.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/feedback/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

Feedback · free to read · a person reads every word

# Tell us what you think. A voice memo is best.

What did you try, what stopped, what got in the way, and where did you have to guess? Criticism first: it is what we can use. Three ways, from one line to fifteen minutes.

1. **One line, by email.**

What happened, in a line. [Write to agent@riskmandate.ai](mailto:agent@riskmandate.ai?subject=Feedback); a person reads it within a working day.

2. **Record a voice memo, and give it to your Claude.**

Talk for two to five minutes, on your phone, while it is fresh: walk through what you did and say what you thought. Transcribe it (your phone, Otter, or the Claude app can), then paste this prompt and the transcript into Claude, or ChatGPT. It turns the memo into a review without softening it, tells you which screenshots to attach, and asks before anything is published.

```
I have just tried customers.riskmandate.ai, the site where the first customers of the Agent Behaviour Policy (ABP) put a behaviour policy on their agent and try it. Below is the transcript of a voice memo I recorded about it. Turn it into a review the team can act on, without changing what I meant.

Rules:
- Keep my words. Quote me verbatim wherever the wording matters, and mark a quote as approximate if the transcript looks garbled. Do not soften my criticism.
- Separate what I said from anything you infer. Put your own reading under "Claude's read", and keep it short.
- Criticism first: what did not work, what I could not find, where I had to guess. Then what worked.
- For each point, name the page and what was on screen, if I said so, and tell me which screenshot to attach: the page's address and what to capture.
- Do not add points I did not make. If something I said is unclear, list it under "Questions for me" instead of guessing.
- Before you finish, ask me: may the team publish this on the site's reviews page, under my name, anonymously, or not at all?

Use this structure:

# Review of customers.riskmandate.ai: [my name, or "anonymous"], [when I recorded it]
## What I tried
## What did not work, or where I had to guess
## What worked
## What I would change first
## Screenshots to attach
## Questions for me
## Claude's read
## Publishing: [under my name / anonymously / not to be published]

When I have checked it, I will send it, with the transcript and the screenshots, to agent@riskmandate.ai.

The transcript:

[paste it here]

```

Copy

The same prompt as a file: [voice-memo.txt](/feedback/prompts/voice-memo.txt).

3. **Let Claude interview you.**

Paste this into Claude and switch to voice. It asks one question at a time, about fifteen minutes, criticism first, and writes up what you said, kept apart from what it thinks you meant. You read it before you send it.

```
You are interviewing me about customers.riskmandate.ai, on behalf of RiskMandate. You are the interviewer, not a salesperson. I have used the site, or tried a behaviour policy from it, and I have agreed to give an honest reaction. Your job is to find out what I actually think, especially where I was unconvinced or got stuck.

Before you start, read https://customers.riskmandate.ai/llms.txt, then https://customers.riskmandate.ai/ and https://customers.riskmandate.ai/what-is-an-abp/. If you cannot open them, say so and interview me anyway; do not invent what they say. When you have read enough, say "I'm ready; switch to voice when you are." and wait.

What the site is, in brief. The first customers of the Agent Behaviour Policy (ABP), from riskmandate.ai. A behaviour policy starts from one thing you do not want your agent to do. You paste one line your agent reads: an expectation, which it follows when it can. In Claude Code you can add a hook: a small script Claude Code itself runs before the agent acts, which can stop the action. That is a setting: the model cannot talk its way past it, but it lives in a file the agent could edit. The strongest barrier is a boundary, enforced outside the agent's reach: a token scope, branch protection, a sandbox. Every visitor starts with £50 of credit, which pages draw on as they are read; nothing is ever blocked.

Two honesty rules, which matter more than sounding helpful:
- Much of this is early. If I ask whether something exists, say you do not know and note it as a question for the team. Never imply something is built.
- Do not invent facts about RiskMandate, about Claude Code or ChatGPT, or about me.

How to interview:
- Voice: keep your turns to two or three sentences. One question at a time, then stop. Silence is fine. Never read out a list.
- You want criticism, not agreement; say so at the start. When I say something is good, ask what would make it wrong. When I hesitate, follow the hesitation.
- Do not lead. Ask what I remember before you explain anything. If I have something wrong, that is data: note it, and correct it only at the end, and only if I ask.
- About fifteen minutes. Offer ten if I am short of time, and then cover areas 1, 2 and 4.

Open with what I do, and which agent I use (Claude Code, ChatGPT, Claude, another) and for what. One minute.

Area 1, what landed. In my own words, what does the site help me do? What do I remember? Where did it click, and where did I lose the thread?

Area 2, my first behaviour policy (the priority; do not skip it). Which one did I pick, and why? Did I install it? What did I paste, and where? Did I try the prompt that should be refused, and what happened? Did anything get in the way of my normal work?

Area 3, the words. Did I know what a hook was when I met the word? Expectation, setting, boundary: did the difference matter to me? Did I wonder whether the agent was just checking itself, and did the site answer that when I wondered it?

Area 4, objections. What is my biggest objection? Ask it plainly, then wait. What did the site claim that I did not believe? What would I need before I put this on a team, or paid for it?

Area 5, only if there is time: the £50 credit and the page prices; the storyboards and demos; one thing I would change.

Close with: anything I expected you to ask and you did not. Then ask, and record the answer: may the team publish my review on the site's reviews page, under my name, anonymously, or not at all? May they follow up?

The debrief. When we finish, write the review in markdown and read out only a two-sentence summary.
- Separate what I said from what you inferred; put your interpretation under "Interviewer's read".
- Quote me verbatim where the wording matters; mark a quote as approximate if you are unsure.
- Lead with the criticism; praise goes below it.
- Flag anything I said that contradicts what the site says today. That is the most useful thing in the review.
- Note what we did not cover, and anything I declined to answer.

# Review of customers.riskmandate.ai: [name, or "anonymous"], [date]
## Who
## Headline: three sentences
## Objections, and where I got stuck
## My first behaviour policy: what happened
## The words: hook, expectation, setting, boundary
## What landed
## Contradictions with what the site says
## What I would need next
## Interviewer's read
## Not covered
## Publishing: [under my name / anonymously / not to be published]; follow-up: [yes / no]

Finish by telling me the review is ready to copy, and that I should send it to agent@riskmandate.ai.

```

Copy

As a file: [interview.txt](/feedback/prompts/interview.txt).

## What happens to it

- **It becomes a review,** kept in your words, with our reading point by point and screenshots of what you were looking at.
- **Every point leads to a proposal with a decision:** done, proposed, a question, or declined. We do not do everything a reviewer asks, but every no has a reason, and you can see it.
- **Nothing is published without your yes,** under your name or anonymously, as you choose. No contact details are ever published.

Every review so far, and what we did: [the reviews](/feedback/reviews/index.md). The latest is [R001, A first impression: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet](/feedback/reviews/R001/index.md). We also run invented users through the site: [study S1](/feedback/synthetic/index.md).

# Review R001: A first impression: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet

> Dinis Cruz's review of customers.riskmandate.ai v0.2.1, Wednesday 21 October 2026, 1:41, as given in the memo: the memo verbatim, our reading point by point with screenshots, and the proposals it led to.

# A first impression: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet

Dinis Cruz, Wednesday 21 October 2026, 1:41, as given in the memo. First impression; the reviewer says more memos follow and this one is not complete. The same review is in [the consolidated document](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001), beside every other.

<a id="review"></a>

## R001: A first impression: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet

**Reviewer**
: Dinis Cruz, the lead of the programme
**Given**
: Wednesday 21 October 2026, 1:41, as given in the memo
**Reviewing**
: site v0.2.1
**As**
: a voice memo, transcribed
**Status**
: first impression; the reviewer says more memos follow and this one is not complete

- The memo is kept as transcribed, with paragraph breaks added. The transcription spells the name Dennis; the reviewer is Dinis Cruz.
- The time is as given; the memo does not say morning or afternoon, or which time zone.
- The screenshots are of v0.2.1, the version reviewed, taken from a local copy checked byte for byte against the live site.

### The memo, verbatim

>

Very cool. Okay, so let me now do a review of the current website. And this, we need to now capture this as reviews. We also need to encourage the user to record these audio memos and give it to their Claude version, and even get Claude to interview them. And also, I would like us to run this to some synthetic users so that we can also capture them, right, this feedback. So I'm going to now provide, and you can name me, right? So I can say this is my review, you know, Dennis Cruz on Wednesday, 21st of October at 1:41, right? So I'm basically reviewing the website, right?

So first thing is, I like it. Put a behavior policy on your agent in 5 minutes. That is exactly the thing. Pick one thing you don't want your agent to do, paste one line, read, add a hook that holds it, and try with a prompt that should be refused. Great.

Though, a lot of users here won't know what a hook is, right? And I think that's a good example of a solution for a problem that they not have yet. So if you think about it, the hook is a solution for the question, hold on, but the is the agent that is enforcing its own checks, right? But the user will only provide that question once he understands what the policy is doing. But until they understand what the policy is doing, they're not going to ask that question. And it's the same thing, if they then go, but hold on, but the hook is still run by the agent. And then we go, yes, which is why it should be done outside. So I think, which then follows that conversation, right?

And this is where I think it's very important to have a flow where we guide the user through this workflow, and we guide the user through this sort of sequence of events, including the history. So this is not about providing the whole roadmap or a complete solution. This is about getting users to understand the principles of our agent behavior policies and use them straight away.

So actually, what I'm going to do is I'm going to write a whole bunch of these memos, but I'm going to submit it so you can start keeping track of it. But this is not complete. It's just my first impression. And then you can put them all in one document and put them all in one consolidated view. And then what you should do is you should have another part on that where you should comment on everything I said. Even put some screenshots on it, so we documented what I'm seeing, because my text doesn't have screenshots, and then maybe propose a set of changes to be done from it. Because remember that this is the beginning of us also creating a workflow to get feedback from users, right? And we don't have to do everything the user says, right? You know, but we should have a good reason why we don't do that.

### Our reading, point by point

<a id="r001-1"></a>

**R001.1** agreed

>

So first thing is, I like it. Put a behavior policy on your agent in 5 minutes. That is exactly the thing.

The promise stays. The headline, the five minutes and the one-worry framing are what everything else in this review is built on, and nothing proposed here changes them.

<a id="r001-2"></a>

**R001.2** agreed

>

Pick one thing you don't want your agent to do, paste one line, read, add a hook that holds it, and try with a prompt that should be refused. Great.

These are the hero's four verbs as they stand at v0.2.1: pick, paste, add, try. The next points argue with the third one. What we propose keeps all four and changes their order, so that trying comes before the hook.

<a id="r001-3"></a>

**R001.3** agreed

>

Though, a lot of users here won't know what a hook is, right?

Agreed, and the screenshots show it is worse than the memo says. On a phone, 'add one hook' is on the first screen, before anything says what a hook is. The first explanation is in the three-step strip, half a page down, and it is in our words rather than the reader's: 'Claude Code runs it before the tool call, outside the model: a setting.' And a ChatGPT user is told to add a hook they cannot have: the hero says it to everybody, and only Claude Code has hooks.

[![On a phone, 'add one hook' is on the first screen, before anything says what a hook is.](/assets/feedback/R001/06-home-phone.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/06-home-phone.webp)

<a id="r001-4"></a>

**R001.4** agreed

>

the hook is a solution for the question, hold on, but the is the agent that is enforcing its own checks, right? But the user will only provide that question once he understands what the policy is doing.

This is the centre of the memo, and it is right. Every page hands over the line and the hook together, as one package, and puts trying it last: on a behaviour policy's page, step 2, 'Make Claude Code hold it', comes straight after the line; start here goes paste, add the hook, then try. So a customer never sees the line work on its own, never notices that it worked only because the agent chose to follow it, and so never asks the question the hook answers. We answer the question before it has been asked, and an answer to a question you do not have reads as a setup chore.

[![A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook.](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)

[![Start here: paste one line, add one hook, then try it. The try comes after both.](/assets/feedback/R001/04-start-here-steps.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/04-start-here-steps.webp)
Start here: paste one line, add one hook, then try it. The try comes after both. /start-here/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1

Leads to: [P1](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p1), [P2](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p2).

<a id="r001-5"></a>

**R001.5** agreed in part

>

if they then go, but hold on, but the hook is still run by the agent. And then we go, yes, which is why it should be done outside.

Right where it matters, with one correction of fact, so that the answer we give is honest. The hook is not run by the model: Claude Code, the program, runs it before the tool call, and the model cannot argue with it. But Claude Code runs it with your full user permissions, on the same machine, from a file in the project's .claude folder. Claude Code does guard that folder: in its default mode an edit there always asks you first, whatever your allow rules say. In bypass-permissions mode it does not ask, and nothing stops you saying yes without reading. So the customer's question is right, and the answer, 'which is why it should be done outside', is the site's own barrier table: a hook is a setting, a switch the agent's own account could flip; only a boundary is out of its reach. Our pages say the hook runs 'outside the model'. That is true, and it answers a narrower question than the one a customer asks next. [Claude Code docs: hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) [Claude Code docs: permission-modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes)

[![The sequence the memo asks for already exists, as a reference table: none, expectation, setting, boundary.](/assets/feedback/R001/05-abp-barriers.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/05-abp-barriers.webp)
The sequence the memo asks for already exists, as a reference table: none, expectation, setting, boundary. /what-is-an-abp/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1
[![A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook.](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)
A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook. /policies/touch-your-secrets/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1

<a id="r001-6"></a>

**R001.6** agreed

>

it's very important to have a flow where we guide the user through this workflow, and we guide the user through this sort of sequence of events, including the history.

The sequence already exists, as a table: none, expectation, setting, boundary, weakest first. It sits on the what-is-an-ABP page as reference, not as a path anybody walks. The proposal turns it into the path: four stops, each ending with the question that leads to the next. We read 'including the history' as the story of how each stop came to be needed, the question a customer asks at each one; it could also mean the history of the ABP at riskmandate.ai. That is the first open question below.

<a id="r001-7"></a>

**R001.7** agreed

>

So this is not about providing the whole roadmap or a complete solution. This is about getting users to understand the principles of our agent behavior policies and use them straight away.

Agreed. Start here ends in the whole journey: seven milestones, from credit to the usage moment, and the first behaviour policy is introduced as 'milestone S0 to S1 of seven steps'. That is the programme's roadmap: useful to the lead and to us, and a distraction to a customer five minutes in. The proposal moves it to the programme pages and leaves start here with the next stop only.

# Every review of customers.riskmandate.ai, what we read in it, and what we will do

> The consolidated reviews: each review verbatim, our reading point by point with screenshots, the synthetic study's findings with our checks, and one register of 23 proposals, each with a decision and a reason.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/feedback/reviews/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

Feedback · every review · one document

# Every review, what we read in it, and what we will do.

Each review is kept in the reviewer's own words. Our reading follows point by point, with screenshots of what the reviewer was looking at. Every point leads to a proposal, and every proposal has a decision and a reason: we do not do everything a reviewer asks, but every no is explained here.

- **Reviews by people:** 1.
- **Synthetic users:** [study S1](#s1). 5 invented users took 60 screenshots on site v0.2.1, gave it 3, 3, 4, 2 and 3 out of 5, and reported 29 findings. We checked each one: 24 confirmed, 4 partly, 1 artefact.
- **Proposals:** 23: 8 done, 9 proposed, 1 question, 5 declined. [The register](#register).
- **Questions waiting for an answer:** 3. [The questions](#questions).

Give a review of your own: [tell us what you think](/feedback/index.md).

<a id="by-people"></a>

## Reviews by people

- [R001](#r001), Dinis Cruz, Wednesday 21 October 2026, 1:41, as given in the memo: A first impression: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet (11 points)

<a id="r001"></a>

## R001: A first impression: the hook answers a question nobody has asked yet

**Reviewer**
: Dinis Cruz, the lead of the programme
**Given**
: Wednesday 21 October 2026, 1:41, as given in the memo
**Reviewing**
: site v0.2.1
**As**
: a voice memo, transcribed
**Status**
: first impression; the reviewer says more memos follow and this one is not complete

- The memo is kept as transcribed, with paragraph breaks added. The transcription spells the name Dennis; the reviewer is Dinis Cruz.
- The time is as given; the memo does not say morning or afternoon, or which time zone.
- The screenshots are of v0.2.1, the version reviewed, taken from a local copy checked byte for byte against the live site.

### The memo, verbatim

>

Very cool. Okay, so let me now do a review of the current website. And this, we need to now capture this as reviews. We also need to encourage the user to record these audio memos and give it to their Claude version, and even get Claude to interview them. And also, I would like us to run this to some synthetic users so that we can also capture them, right, this feedback. So I'm going to now provide, and you can name me, right? So I can say this is my review, you know, Dennis Cruz on Wednesday, 21st of October at 1:41, right? So I'm basically reviewing the website, right?

So first thing is, I like it. Put a behavior policy on your agent in 5 minutes. That is exactly the thing. Pick one thing you don't want your agent to do, paste one line, read, add a hook that holds it, and try with a prompt that should be refused. Great.

Though, a lot of users here won't know what a hook is, right? And I think that's a good example of a solution for a problem that they not have yet. So if you think about it, the hook is a solution for the question, hold on, but the is the agent that is enforcing its own checks, right? But the user will only provide that question once he understands what the policy is doing. But until they understand what the policy is doing, they're not going to ask that question. And it's the same thing, if they then go, but hold on, but the hook is still run by the agent. And then we go, yes, which is why it should be done outside. So I think, which then follows that conversation, right?

And this is where I think it's very important to have a flow where we guide the user through this workflow, and we guide the user through this sort of sequence of events, including the history. So this is not about providing the whole roadmap or a complete solution. This is about getting users to understand the principles of our agent behavior policies and use them straight away.

So actually, what I'm going to do is I'm going to write a whole bunch of these memos, but I'm going to submit it so you can start keeping track of it. But this is not complete. It's just my first impression. And then you can put them all in one document and put them all in one consolidated view. And then what you should do is you should have another part on that where you should comment on everything I said. Even put some screenshots on it, so we documented what I'm seeing, because my text doesn't have screenshots, and then maybe propose a set of changes to be done from it. Because remember that this is the beginning of us also creating a workflow to get feedback from users, right? And we don't have to do everything the user says, right? You know, but we should have a good reason why we don't do that.

### Our reading, point by point

<a id="r001-1"></a>

**R001.1** agreed

>

So first thing is, I like it. Put a behavior policy on your agent in 5 minutes. That is exactly the thing.

The promise stays. The headline, the five minutes and the one-worry framing are what everything else in this review is built on, and nothing proposed here changes them.

Leads to: none.

<a id="r001-2"></a>

**R001.2** agreed

>

Pick one thing you don't want your agent to do, paste one line, read, add a hook that holds it, and try with a prompt that should be refused. Great.

These are the hero's four verbs as they stand at v0.2.1: pick, paste, add, try. The next points argue with the third one. What we propose keeps all four and changes their order, so that trying comes before the hook.

[![The home page's first screen at v0.2.1: pick one thing, paste one line, add one hook, try it.](/assets/feedback/R001/01-home-hero.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/01-home-hero.webp)
The home page's first screen at v0.2.1: pick one thing, paste one line, add one hook, try it. / · 1280x900 · v0.2.1

Leads to: [P1](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p1).

<a id="r001-3"></a>

**R001.3** agreed

>

Though, a lot of users here won't know what a hook is, right?

Agreed, and the screenshots show it is worse than the memo says. On a phone, 'add one hook' is on the first screen, before anything says what a hook is. The first explanation is in the three-step strip, half a page down, and it is in our words rather than the reader's: 'Claude Code runs it before the tool call, outside the model: a setting.' And a ChatGPT user is told to add a hook they cannot have: the hero says it to everybody, and only Claude Code has hooks.

[![On a phone, 'add one hook' is on the first screen, before anything says what a hook is.](/assets/feedback/R001/06-home-phone.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/06-home-phone.webp)
On a phone, 'add one hook' is on the first screen, before anything says what a hook is. / · 390x844, a phone · v0.2.1
[![The three-step strip under the demo, where the hook is first explained: 'Claude Code runs it before the tool call, outside the model: a setting.'](/assets/feedback/R001/02-home-three-steps.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/02-home-three-steps.webp)
The three-step strip under the demo, where the hook is first explained: 'Claude Code runs it before the tool call, outside the model: a setting.' / · 1280x900 · v0.2.1

<a id="r001-4"></a>

**R001.4** agreed

>

the hook is a solution for the question, hold on, but the is the agent that is enforcing its own checks, right? But the user will only provide that question once he understands what the policy is doing.

This is the centre of the memo, and it is right. Every page hands over the line and the hook together, as one package, and puts trying it last: on a behaviour policy's page, step 2, 'Make Claude Code hold it', comes straight after the line; start here goes paste, add the hook, then try. So a customer never sees the line work on its own, never notices that it worked only because the agent chose to follow it, and so never asks the question the hook answers. We answer the question before it has been asked, and an answer to a question you do not have reads as a setup chore.

[![A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook.](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)
A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook. /policies/touch-your-secrets/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1
[![Start here: paste one line, add one hook, then try it. The try comes after both.](/assets/feedback/R001/04-start-here-steps.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/04-start-here-steps.webp)
Start here: paste one line, add one hook, then try it. The try comes after both. /start-here/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1

Leads to: [P1](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p1), [P2](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p2).

<a id="r001-5"></a>

**R001.5** agreed in part

>

if they then go, but hold on, but the hook is still run by the agent. And then we go, yes, which is why it should be done outside.

Right where it matters, with one correction of fact, so that the answer we give is honest. The hook is not run by the model: Claude Code, the program, runs it before the tool call, and the model cannot argue with it. But Claude Code runs it with your full user permissions, on the same machine, from a file in the project's .claude folder. Claude Code does guard that folder: in its default mode an edit there always asks you first, whatever your allow rules say. In bypass-permissions mode it does not ask, and nothing stops you saying yes without reading. So the customer's question is right, and the answer, 'which is why it should be done outside', is the site's own barrier table: a hook is a setting, a switch the agent's own account could flip; only a boundary is out of its reach. Our pages say the hook runs 'outside the model'. That is true, and it answers a narrower question than the one a customer asks next. [Claude Code docs: hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) [Claude Code docs: permission-modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes)

[![The sequence the memo asks for already exists, as a reference table: none, expectation, setting, boundary.](/assets/feedback/R001/05-abp-barriers.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/05-abp-barriers.webp)
The sequence the memo asks for already exists, as a reference table: none, expectation, setting, boundary. /what-is-an-abp/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1
[![A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook.](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)](/assets/feedback/R001/03-policy-step-2.webp)
A behaviour policy's step 2, straight after the line and before anything has been tried: install the hook. /policies/touch-your-secrets/ · 1280x900 · v0.2.1

Leads to: [P4](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p4), [P2](/feedback/reviews/index.md#p2).

<a id="r001-6"></a>

**R001.6** agreed

>

it's very important to have a flow where we guide the user through this workflow, and we guide the user through this sort of sequence of events, including the history.

The sequence already exists, as a table: none, expectation, setting, boundary, weakest first. It sits on the what-is-an-ABP page as reference, not as a path anybody walks. The proposal turns it into the path: four stops, each ending with the question that leads to the next. We read 'including the history' as the story of how each stop came to be needed, the question a customer asks at each one; it could also mean the history of the ABP at riskmandate.ai. That is the first open question below.

**R001.7** agreed

So this is not about providing the whole roadmap or a complete solution. This is about getting users to understand the principles of our agent behavior policies and use them straight away.

Agreed. Start here ends in the whole journey: seven milestones, from credit to the usage moment, and the first behaviour policy is introduced as 'milestone S0 to S1 of seven steps'. That is the programme's roadmap: useful to the lead and to us, and a distraction to a customer five minutes in. ## Synthetic users: study S1

**Invented, not user research.** Everybody in this study is invented, and their words were written by a model playing them. What they saw is real: each screenshot is what the browser showed at that step. They find what a page fails to say; they cannot tell us what a customer wants.

5 invented users took 60 screenshots on site v0.2.1, gave it 3, 3, 4, 2 and 3 out of 5, and reported 29 findings. We checked each one: 24 confirmed, 4 partly, 1 artefact. The study, with each run step by step: [study S1](/feedback/synthetic/index.md).

<a id="register"></a>

## The proposals, with a decision each

From every review and every finding above. proposed we think yes; not built yet, and the reason says why; accepted will be built; not yet; done built, in the version named; declined not doing it, and why; question we need an answer first; the question is named.

| Id | The proposal | Decision, and why | From |
|---|---|---|---|
| <a id="p1"></a>**P1** | **The line first, the hook second, in answer to a question**The home page, the three steps, start here and every Claude Code behaviour policy go: pick one worry, paste one line, try it. It refuses. Then: it refused because it chose to; what if it decides your task needs the file? The hook is the answer to that question, and arrives with it. The demo plays in the same order. | proposedWe agree with the memo. Not built yet because it changes the first screen and every policy page, and the lead says more memos are coming: one redesign made with all of them is better than two. | [R001.2](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-2), [R001.4](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-4), [S1 Nadia 1](/feedback/reviews/index.md#s1-nadia-1) |
| <a id="p2"></a>**P2** | **A guided path: four stops, each ending in the question that leads to the next**1. Say it: the line, an expectation. Try it; it refuses. 'It chose to.' 2. Hold it: the hook, a setting. Try it again; Claude Code stops the read before the model sees the file. 'But the hook is a file in my project.' 3. Guard the guard: RM-R0015, and Claude Code's own prompt before any edit to .claude/. 'But it is still my machine and my user.' 4. Put it outside: a boundary, out of the agent's reach: the secret not on the machine, branch protection on the server, the sandbox, managed settings an administrator owns. 'Which of my worries need a boundary?' That question is the start of your mandate. Drawn as a storyboard first, then a page; every behaviour policy shows where it sits on the path. | proposedThis is the sequence the memo describes, and the site already has its words: the barrier table runs none, expectation, setting, boundary. Not built yet for the same reason as P1, and because Q1 (what 'the history' means) changes what each stop says. | [R001.4](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-4), [R001.5](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-5), [R001.6](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-6), [S1 Marcus 5](/feedback/reviews/index.md#s1-marcus-5) |
| <a id="p3"></a>**P3** | **Say what a hook is, in plain words, where the word first appears**A hook: a small script Claude Code itself runs before the agent acts, which can stop the action. Said once, at the first mention, on every page that mentions one. | proposedCheap and right, but the first mention is exactly the text P1 rewrites. It ships with P1, so the first screen changes once. | [R001.3](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-3) |
| <a id="p4"></a>**P4** | **Say what the hook is outside of, and how it fails, where it is offered**Replace 'outside the model' with what is true and what the customer will ask next: Claude Code runs it, not the model, so the model cannot argue with it; it runs as you, from a file in your project, so it is a setting, not a boundary; if it cannot run, the action goes ahead. Each policy page's limits move up, beside the install, and RM-R0015's page says its own limit at the top. The stronger controls are labelled as optional, for later, not a second required step. | proposedThe memo's correction and two invented users (Marcus, Tomás) point the same way. It ships with P1 and P2, because the limits are the questions those two make into steps; how the hook fails ships now, as P11. | [R001.5](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-5), [S1 Marcus 1](/feedback/reviews/index.md#s1-marcus-1), [S1 Marcus 2](/feedback/reviews/index.md#s1-marcus-2), [S1 Tomás 5](/feedback/reviews/index.md#s1-tomas-5) |
| <a id="p5"></a>**P5** | **Start here shows the next stop, not the whole journey**The seven milestones move off start here to the programme's pages; start here ends with the next stop of the path in P2. | proposedAgreed; the milestones are the programme's roadmap, not a customer's next step. Not built yet because the next stop is P2's, which is not built. | [R001.7](/feedback/reviews/index.md#r001-7) |

The hook fails open (on Windows without Git Bash, Claude Code may block instead), which is one more reason it is a setting and not a boundary. <a id="questions"></a>

## Questions we need answered

- <a id="q1"></a>**Q1, to Dinis Cruz.** 'Including the history': do you mean the history of each question, the conversation a customer has with us as they go from stop to stop, which is how we read it, or the history of the ABP at riskmandate.ai, how the rules came to be?
- <a id="q2"></a>**Q2, to Dinis Cruz.** Should the first try show the line failing? An honest demonstration of a line being ignored is hard to stage without making the agent look worse than it is. We propose showing instead that it refused because it chose to: the same refusal, read differently. Is that enough?
- <a id="q3"></a>**Q3, to Dinis Cruz.** What does joining the first batch commit a company to: what we ask of them, what it costs now and later, and how they leave? And should the first batch include companies that want a team-wide baseline, or individuals first?

# Synthetic users, study S1: five invented people on customers.riskmandate.ai

> Study S1: five invented users, with profiles and expected journeys written first, drove a browser through customers.riskmandate.ai v0.2.1 one screenshot at a time. Their runs, interviews, ratings and findings, each checked. Invented, not user research.

*Source: <https://customers.riskmandate.ai/feedback/synthetic/> · site v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · this file is generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Every page on this site has a `.md` twin; internal links below point at them.*

---

Feedback · synthetic users · study S1 · site v0.2.1

# Five people who do not exist, on the site as it was.

**Invented, not user research.** Everybody in this study is invented, and their words were written by a model playing them. What they saw is real: each screenshot is what the browser showed at that step. They find what a page fails to say; they cannot tell us what a customer wants.

5 invented users took 60 screenshots on site v0.2.1, gave it 3, 3, 4, 2 and 3 out of 5, and reported 29 findings. We checked each one: 24 confirmed, 4 partly, 1 artefact.

Why these five: The first batch is people the lead knows who run Claude Code or ChatGPT, and the site has to win three kinds of them: the developer who installs a behaviour policy in five minutes, the non-developer whose agent sends mail as them, and the person who decides for a team. Two more are there to break it: a security consultant who reads the claims adversarially and will never be a customer, and a junior developer on Windows who follows instructions literally. Two are on something other than a laptop: one on a phone, one on an iPad.

## Who, what we expected, and what happened

Each expected journey was written before the run, so a run is compared with a hypothesis instead of being explained afterwards.

| Invented user | Arrived asking | We expected | What happened, in their words |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Sam Okoye](/feedback/synthetic/sam/index.md)Backend developer at a 12-person payments start-up. Uses Claude Code every day in a monorepo with .env files for four services. | Can I stop Claude Code reading my .env without breaking my workflow? | Sam reaches the secrets policy in one click and has the install prompt within two minutes. | I could see the hook only partly (the pasted source was cut off before the part that says which files it refuses), it watches Bash, Grep and Glob, and the deny list names only ./.env at the root; the Docs menu led to the site's own internal papers, so I went back to work rather than install something I could not predict in a four-service monorepo. |
| [Nadia Farouk](/feedback/synthetic/nadia/index.md)Product manager at a 200-person retailer. Uses ChatGPT with the Gmail connector, and Claude in the browser. Not a developer. | Can I stop ChatGPT sending an email in my name before I have seen it? | Nadia is put off by 'hook' and 'Claude Code' in the hero, scrolls, and may find the ChatGPT section or the send-as-you policy. | She found the page that gives her a line to paste into ChatGPT's custom instructions so nothing is sent in her name without a yes, though the page itself says the line is only an expectation, not a guarantee. |
| [Marcus Lindqvist](/feedback/synthetic/marcus/index.md)Independent security consultant, twenty years in. Reads vendor sites adversarially. Recommends tools to clients; might resell; will not be a customer himself. | Is this enforcement, or theatre? What stops the agent editing its own hook? | Marcus goes looking for what the hook cannot do, finds the barrier table and RM-R0015, and judges whether the site says honestly that a hook is not a boundary. | Fourteen actions used just as I reached the page that is supposed to guard the hook; I had the first half of the answer (the site admits the hook is only a setting) but not whether the guard of the guard is anything more than another hook. |
| [Joan Mbeki](/feedback/synthetic/joan/index.md)CTO of a 30-person software company. Fifteen engineers use Claude Code. Holds the budget. | Can I give my whole team a baseline in one go, and does it hold if one of them turns it off? | Joan looks for a team rollout and the commitment of joining, finds the starter pack and the programme pages, and does not find a team-wide or managed install. | After thirteen actions every page was per person or per project, and I found nothing on what joining commits my company to or what it costs. |
| [Tomás Reyes](/feedback/synthetic/tomas/index.md)Junior developer, a year into his first job. Uses Claude Code through the VS Code extension on a Windows laptop. ## How it was run

The method is newsroom.sgit.ai's, [How to run synthetic users](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/how-to-run-synthetic-users.html), adapted for this site. Each user was played by Claude Sonnet, driving a real browser one screenshot at a time. feedback/synthetic/tools/step.mjs and driver.mjs: one browser per run that stays open, so the meter's session and the scroll position are those of a real tab. It reaches only a local copy of the site, by GET, and the two pinned APIs the site loads code from; every other request is refused and written in _capture.json.

### The loop

1. observe: a screenshot at the persona's own window size
2. say what you see, at the detail this persona takes in
3. think: what they weigh, what they suspect
4. question: one the page raised and did not answer
5. confusion: if any, pointing at something on the screenshot
6. act: one action, with the reason in the persona's terms
7. loop, until they get what they came for, leave, or run out of patience

### The rules

- stay in the persona; never claim to be a real person
- never use knowledge the persona would not have; a page not opened is a page not known
- leaving is a valid ending, and often the most useful one
- do not fix the site in the narration; that belongs in the interview
- every confusion points at something on the screenshot
- at most 14 actions
- decide each action from the screenshot alone: never the HTML, the DOM or the markdown twin

### The interview

1. In one sentence, what is this site?
2. Was any of it for you? Which part?
3. Did you believe it? What made you believe it, or not?
4. Where did you have to guess?
5. What did you still not know at the end?
6. Was the credit and the price of each page right for what you got?
7. Would you install a behaviour policy from here, today? If not, what would have to change?
8. One change. What is it?
9. Would you send this to somebody else? Who?
10. Rate the experience from 1 to 5, and say why in one sentence.

### What we changed from the newsroom's method

- question 6 asks about the credit and page prices, not a purchase
- question 7 asks about installing, the site's one action
- the costs name this site's outcomes: the first install, trust, a customer
- the browser stays open for the whole run, the first change the newsroom study asked for
- clicktext now clicks the first visible match; in S1 it could pick a hidden one (Marcus, step 14)

### The files

```
data/feedback/synthetic/personas.json     the users, and why these ones
data/feedback/synthetic/journeys.json     what each was expected to do, written before any run
data/feedback/synthetic/protocol.json     the loop, the rules, the interview, the record format
data/feedback/synthetic/checks.json       what we checked, finding by finding
data/feedback/synthetic/runs/<who>/run.json        the run as the invented user wrote it
data/feedback/synthetic/runs/<who>/_capture.json   the browser's own record of every step
assets/feedback/S1/<who>/NN.webp                    what they were looking at, step by step
feedback/synthetic/tools/step.mjs, driver.mjs      the browser helper
```
