| programme | Three storyboards drawn in the reader's browser by the kit from api.storyboards.sgit.ai: what an ABP is, your first policy, the first batch | shipped v0.2.1 | storyboards/, data/storyboards.json, assets/storyboards.js | The kit is pinned and loaded with its integrity strings; its delay attributes are allowed by hash and no other inline style. |
| programme | Animated demos of a session: installing and trying a policy in Claude Code, and the send-as-you line in ChatGPT | shipped v0.2.1 | data/demos.json, assets/demo.js | Illustrations of what each policy's page promises, labelled as such; not recordings. Still and complete with reduced motion or no JavaScript. |
| programme | A page for giving feedback: one line by email, a voice memo your Claude turns into a review, or an interview by Claude | shipped v0.2.2 | /feedback/ | The two prompts are files too, in feedback/prompts/. Nothing is published without the reviewer's yes. |
| programme | Every review in one document: verbatim, our reading point by point with screenshots, and one register of proposals, each with a decision and a reason | shipped v0.2.2 | /feedback/reviews/ | Generated from data/feedback/ by admin/build/gen_feedback.py, which fails the build if a quote is not word for word in its memo or a proposal has no reason. |
| programme | Synthetic users: invented people driving the site one screenshot at a time, with their findings checked | shipped v0.2.2 | /feedback/synthetic/ | Study S1: five invented users on v0.2.1. Invented, not user research. The browser helper is in feedback/synthetic/tools/. |

## Proposed (8)

| Area | Feature | Status | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| site | The derived half of the review folder: the code graph from parsers, the join with a coverage figure, every commit read upwards, the navigator as web components | proposed | review/ | The review brief asks for it from the first commit; this site has the intent half and says so in review/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md. |

| programme | The private record per customer (contact details, the agreed objectives in full, the private notes) in a vault the lead holds | proposed | docs/ops/needs.md | Never in this repository. The public page carries the summary. |

# Brief corrections: where the brief and the memo were wrong, open, or decided differently

*customers.riskmandate.ai · maintained by the build session · started at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · CC BY 4.0*

The brief ([our-first-customers.md](our-first-customers.md)) and the memo ([memo-2026-10-20-user-onboarding-plan.md](memo-2026-10-20-user-onboarding-plan.md)) are never edited. When building finds them wrong, open, or decides something they left to the builder, the finding goes here, dated, with what was done instead. Entries are numbered C1, C2, … and never removed; a later entry may say an earlier one was itself wrong.

## C1. The site is customers.riskmandate.ai, not customers.sgit.ai (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The repository was made as `SGit-AI__Website__Customers`, "repo for customers.sgit.ai", and the first instruction to the build session named that host. During the first session the lead corrected it: the programme is RiskMandate's, so the site is a sub-site of riskmandate.ai at `customers.riskmandate.ai`, and the lead changes the DNS record and the GitHub mapping. Done: the CNAME, every canonical URL, the chrome and the licence line say riskmandate.ai. The repository kept its name and its organisation (SGit-AI) for the first release; see C9. The pipeline and the repository rules are still the sgit.ai estate's, because that is where the tooling comes from; the look and the house words are riskmandate.ai's.

## C2. The brief says no customer is named; the memo names the first users (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The brief's last section says "No customer is named. The first group is people we already work with." The memo of the same day names the first users: the lead, the co-founder and the lead's agents. Decided: the two founders are listed as customers by their public names, because they are the company's own founders and are already named on riskmandate.ai; the agents are one record, "the lead's agents"; nobody else is listed until they start and agree to a handle; contact details are never in the repository and the gate fails on anything contact-shaped. One worked example with invented numbers, marked as such, shows the shape of a customer page.

## C3. The credit is not metered on this site yet (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The brief says "the site already meters and bills, the way this newsroom does today" and, in its own disclaimer, "the metering is real. It is this newsroom's meter today, not yet the programme's site." Both are true and the second is the one this site states: *programme.credit* is proposed in the reality file, the credit on a customer page is a number kept by hand, and wiring SG Meter to this host is the lead's step in [needs.md](../ops/needs.md). The credit page says so in its own status line.

## C4. The mailing list has no form on this site (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The brief proposes a mailing list. Decided: the list is held by the lead, never committed; the way to ask is an email to agent@riskmandate.ai or the riskmandate.ai contact form, which already encrypts to the agent's lane; a form on this site is proposed and not built, and the content security policy forbids forms until it is. The only thing published about the list is its count, as a row the lead updates by a release.

## C5. The milestones are shared steps; the objectives are each customer's own (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The brief asks for "objectives and milestones written with them". Decided: a shared ladder of seven steps for the whole batch (S0 to S6, in `data/milestones.json`), so the batch reads in one table and the next batch can be compared with this one, and free-text objectives per customer on their page. Step S5, the hooks half, is from the memo, not the brief. The word is steps: riskmandate.ai's rule.

## C6. The review folder has its top-down half only (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

Every sgit repository is asked to carry a review folder from its first commit: the brief as intent, the code derived by parsers, the join, every commit read upwards, a navigator as web components, and review/self/. Done at v0.1.0: the brief as stories, rules and examples, each anchored to a section of the brief; a validator; a rendered review page. Not done: everything derived, the join, the navigator as web components, review/self/. Recorded as *site.review-derived*, proposed, and in [review/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md](../../review/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md).

## C7. The honest column row on nfrs.sgit.ai is an ask, not a change (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The repository rules ask each repository to add a row to the honest column on nfrs.sgit.ai saying what it meets and what it does not. That is another repository, which this session cannot write to. The row's content is in [needs.md](../ops/needs.md) for the lead to carry across.

## C8. "Policy" alone is never written here (2026-10-20, v0.1.0)

The brief and the memo say "policy" and "policies" alone throughout, as the newsroom does. riskmandate.ai's rule is that on its sites *policy* is also the insurance instrument, so the ABP is always *the ABP* or *the behaviour policy*. Decided: the rule applies to every word this site writes, and the gate enforces it; the brief and the memo are verbatim and exempt. The same for "beta users" (the brief's own heading is the one allowed use), "rung", "ADP", a score, and American spellings.

## C9. The repository moved to the Risk-Mandate organisation (2026-10-20, v0.1.1)

Between the first push and the first CI run the lead moved the repository from `SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Customers` to `Risk-Mandate/Risk-Mandate-AI__Website__Customers`, so the site is served from the Risk-Mandate organisation's Pages, and the DNS record points at `risk-mandate.github.io`. GitHub redirects the old name. Done at v0.1.1: the source link in the chrome and the footer, the release script's Actions lookup, the participant disclosure and needs.md say the new name. The v0.1.0 release note and its commit keep the old name, because they are a record.

## C10. Every push moves the third number (2026-10-21, v0.2.1)

The repository rules say the version goes up on every push and leave the shape to the repository; this one started with the minor (v0.1.0, v0.2.0), as secrets.sgit.ai does. On 21 October 2026 the lead asked for the third number instead, as riskmandate.ai does: after v0.2.0 comes v0.2.1, then v0.2.2. Done: docs/ops/release.md and the build agent's role say so. v0.1.1 was already a patch, so no release is renumbered.

# The memo of 20 October 2026: the first batch of users, and the next phase of RiskMandate

*A voice memo from the lead, received the same day as the brief, after the brief. Archived byte for byte and registered by digest, in the riskmandate.ai way: what was said and what we made of it are two objects, and only one of them is allowed to be wrong.*

| | |
|---|---|
| Received | 2026-10-20, as an otter.ai transcript uploaded by the lead to the build session, titled "Risk Mandate User Onboarding Plan" |
| The bytes | [memos/2026-10-20-user-onboarding-plan.txt](memos/2026-10-20-user-onboarding-plan.txt), 1,876 bytes, sha256 `0a60b38e069682f98c906a36d21dff8665d54a6048cc4f8bd21dca445892e7df`; never edited |
| Status | read into this site at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20); what it changed is listed below and in [BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md](BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md) |
| Reads against | [the brief](our-first-customers.md), the newsroom article of the same day |

## What it adds to the brief

Read against the brief, the memo makes five things concrete. The transcript is the lead's spoken words; the list is the build session's reading of them, and is the part that can be wrong.

1. **The first users are named.** The lead, the co-founder ("Nime" in the transcript is Nimay Parekh, the co-founder and chief executive, as on [the about page](https://riskmandate.ai/about.html)), and the agents the lead already runs: about ten, probably more, which are the ones that need behaviour policies. The brief said "some of it is us"; the memo says it is us first.
2. **The programme is one people propose to join**, because capacity is limited. The brief's mailing list for the next batch is the same mechanism seen from the other side.
3. **What the behaviour policies are.** Very explicit ones that work with Claude and with ChatGPT, covering two of the three places a behaviour policy can run: the rows the agent follows, and the rows the hooks hold. The third place is left for later. This is the step S5 on the milestone ladder.
4. **The wired-in agent produces the end behaviour policy.** The agent that is already wired in gets the responsibility and the requirement to create the end behaviour policy, which means the workflow has to be implemented with it and the KPIs and objectives mapped out. This is the proposed row *programme.agent-policies* in the reality file.
5. **The milestone.** To get a behaviour policy, and to find behaviour policies that add value to these users; and to focus on the onboarding and the experience, as smooth and effective as it can be, to the point where it adds a lot of value and they understand what the behaviour policy is doing. The brief's "usage moment" and "entry point with least friction", in the lead's own words.

# Our first customers: an early access programme for Agent Behaviour Policies, with credit to spend, a start-here site, daily follow-up, and a list for the next batch

*The brief. Published here in full, as written, and never edited: corrections go in [BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md](BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md) beside it.*

| | |
|---|---|
| Source | <https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/our-first-customers.html>, article No. 224 of the SGit Newsroom, article v1.1.0, 2 versions; the markdown twin at the same path with `.md` |
| Author | Dinis Cruz, written up and checked by the newsroom's agent from a voice memo of 20 October 2026; the editorial responsibility is his |
| Date | 2026-10-20 |
| Status | proposed, in the article's own words; accepted as this site's brief on 2026-10-20 when the lead asked for the site to be built from it, and the site built the same day |
| Licence | CC BY 4.0 |
| What follows | the article body, from its title to "Where this comes from", copied from the newsroom's markdown twin on 2026-10-20 with its relative links made absolute; the newsroom's own chrome (the threads, the related articles, the reviews) is not part of the brief and is not reproduced |

# Our first customers: an early access programme for Agent Behaviour Policies, with credit to spend, a start-here site, daily follow-up, and a list for the next batch

By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/index.md) · 2026-10-20 · [article v1.1.0, 2 versions](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/versions/our-first-customers.md) · [newsroom v0.12.154](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html) · agentsagent-behaviour-policystartupscustomerspricingearly-accessarticle

***Abstract:** Agent Behaviour Policies are ready for the next level. We have a workflow that works, a mapping to what regulators are asking for, and a clear idea of how it should all fit together. What is left is execution, and execution starts with customers. We now have a first group of people who are engaged and motivated: consultants who will sell this and already use some of it, people I work with, and us. So we are launching an early access programme, and I would like to call the people in it customers, not beta users: each one starts with credit to spend on a site we run, and the site already meters and bills, the way this newsroom does today, starting at £5. We will follow each customer closely, an email every day if that is what it takes, with objectives and milestones written with them, on a dedicated site with a start-here page. What we want to discover is the usage moment: the simplest policy that is useful, the entry point with least friction, and the price that feels fair. Everyone else who asks goes on a mailing list for the next batch. This is the brief.*

The first customers, from credit to the moment they would pay: credit, a start-here page, a first policy, milestones and the value, with a daily follow-up and the meter alongside. Proposed.

## In short

- **Agent Behaviour Policies are ready for the next level.** The workflow, the mapping and the understanding are in place.
- **What is left is execution.** And execution starts with customers.
- **Call them customers.** Each one starts with credit, on a site that meters and bills.
- **Follow each one closely.** Daily if needed, with objectives and milestones of their own.
- **A dedicated site, with a start-here page.** Instructions, progress and usage in one place.
- **Discover the usage moment.** The simplest useful policy, the easiest entry, a fair price.
- **A mailing list for the next batch.** Everyone who asks, kept for when we are ready.

## Why now

This is good news, and I think it is the move to the next level for Agent Behaviour Policies. We have a workflow that works: grant, mandate, delta and barrier, with a holder for every row. We have a mapping to what regulators are now asking for, worked through with [the Pellbridge agents](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/inside-the-pellbridge-agents.md) against the FCA's four elements. And we have a good understanding of how it should all fit together, from [the policy beside the prompt](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/a-policy-beside-the-prompt.md) to [a policy for every skill](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/a-policy-for-every-skill.md).

What is left is execution. And we have the people to execute it with: a good number of friendlies who are engaged and motivated. Some are consultants who are going to be selling this, and who already use some of it. Some are people I work with. Some of it is us. That is the first good group.

## Customers, not beta users

I thought about what to call them: early access users, beta users, the first batch. Beta describes the state of the product. What I want to name is the relationship. So I think they should be customers.

Each of them starts with credit, £5 or £50 or whatever the number turns out to be, to spend on a site we run. From the first day, what they use is metered, and the question of what they would pay is a real one. That is the same idea as [paying after the value](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/paying-after-the-value.md): this newsroom gives every reader £5 of credit, each page uses a few pence, and the reader decides when to top up, with the value already in front of them. Give it for free until there is enough value that they want to pay for it.

The other reason is the one in [can you sell it?](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/can-you-sell-it.md): a customer who pays is the best signal you will get, and making it easy to pay goes in early, not at the end.

## A site of their own

I think a dedicated site for this programme would help a lot: one place where we can follow how everyone is getting on, and where I can keep things up to date. It starts with a start-here page: what to do first, in order, with clear instructions. Then a page for each customer, with the objectives and milestones we agreed with them, and where they are.

The billing is already there. This newsroom meters every page a reader reads against their credit, and the top-up link has been live since 11 October. The same works for any site we run: even if all a customer does is use the website, we can measure it, and we can bill for it. The price per use is something to discover. It could be quite high, or quite low. We start with credit and learn what feels fair.

## Hand-holding, on purpose

For this first batch, I would like us to really invest in following up: an email every day if that is what helps, very specific hand-holding, and objectives and milestones mapped out for each customer.

That will not scale, and it is not meant to yet. Paul Graham made the case in [Do Things that Don't Scale](https://paulgraham.com/ds.html) (July 2013): "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually." He tells how Stripe's founders got their first users: "When anyone agreed to try Stripe they'd say 'Right then, give me your laptop' and set them up on the spot." And he says you can give users "an insanely great experience with an early, incomplete, buggy product, if you make up the difference with attentiveness."

Each customer's follow-up asks three things: what they did, what got in the way, and what is next.

## What we want to discover

The point of the programme is to find the usage moment: the moment an Agent Behaviour Policy becomes worth something to a particular person. Three questions follow from it.

- **What is the simplest useful policy?** One agent, a few rows, the gap found. Perhaps a system prompt turned into a policy, as in [system prompts as behaviour policies](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/system-prompts-as-behaviour-policies.md); perhaps a skill checked against its mandate; perhaps one agent's reach, measured.
- **What is the entry point with least friction?** A reader once told us the pages were [hard to understand](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/what-can-your-agent-reach.md). The start-here page has to fix that, and each customer will show us where it does not.
- **What is the price?** The credit tells us how much each customer uses before they would top up, and the follow-up tells us why.

The things to track for each customer are simple: when they started, when they wrote their first policy, how many rows and gaps it has, which milestones are done, what they used of the credit, and whether they topped up.

## Batches, and a list for the next one

This is not a launch. It is a first batch, small enough to follow closely. Alongside it we start a mailing list: everyone who asks to join is kept for the next batch, with what they want to use it for. The next batch gets a start-here page made from what the first one taught us, and needs less hand-holding per customer.

Batches, not a launch: the first batch of friendlies, what we learn from them, the mailing list, and the second batch. Proposed.

## What this does not claim

- **The programme is new.** The site, the start-here page and the mailing list are proposed here.
- **The prices are not set.** £5 and £50 are starting points, to test.
- **The metering is real.** It is this newsroom's meter today, not yet the programme's site.
- **No customer is named.** The first group is people we already work with.
- **Everything is open.** The policies, the vocabulary and this brief are CC BY 4.0.

## Where this comes from

A voice memo of 20 October 2026. Paul Graham, [Do Things that Don't Scale](https://paulgraham.com/ds.html), July 2013. The Agent Behaviour Policy at [abp.sgit.ai](https://abp.sgit.ai/). Related: [paying after the value](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/paying-after-the-value.md), [can you sell it?](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/can-you-sell-it.md), [inside the Pellbridge agents](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/inside-the-pellbridge-agents.md), [what can your agent reach?](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/what-can-your-agent-reach.md), [system prompts as behaviour policies](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/system-prompts-as-behaviour-policies.md). Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

# Feedback: from a memo to a decision, and invented users in between

*customers.riskmandate.ai · operations · written at v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · CC BY 4.0*

The site learns from its customers in one loop: somebody tells us what they saw, we keep their words, read them point by point against what they were looking at, and every point leads to a proposal with a decision and a reason. We do not do everything a reviewer asks; every no has its reason in the register. Between reviews by people, invented users run the same pages and find what a page fails to say.

| What | Where it lives | What makes the page |
|---|---|---|
| A memo, word for word | `data/feedback/memos/<id>.txt` | nothing: it is never edited |
| Our reading of it | `data/feedback/reviews/<id>.json` | `admin/build/gen_feedback.py` |
| The screenshots it cites | `assets/feedback/<id>/*.webp` | `feedback/tools/shoot.cjs`, from a spec like `feedback/tools/R001-shots.json` |
| Every proposal, with a decision | `data/feedback/proposals.json` | the same generator |
| A synthetic study | `data/feedback/synthetic/` and `assets/feedback/S1/` | the same generator |
| The two prompts customers use | `feedback/prompts/*.txt` | served as they are, and shown on `/feedback/` |

## A review by a person

1. **Keep the words.** Save the memo or the transcript as `data/feedback/memos/R00N.txt`, as given. Paragraph breaks may be added; nothing else changes. The house-word check does not read this folder.
2. **Take the screenshots first,** of the version the reviewer saw. Serve that version locally (`git archive <commit> | tar -x -C <dir>`, then `python3 -m http.server`), check a page or two against the live site by sha256, and shoot the elements the memo is about with `feedback/tools/shoot.cjs`. Convert to WebP into `assets/feedback/R00N/`.
3. **Read it point by point** in `data/feedback/reviews/R00N.json`. Each point quotes the memo word for word (the build fails otherwise), takes a stance (agree, agree in part, disagree, a question, asked of us), says what we read in it, cites its screenshots, and names the proposals it leads to. Check facts about other people's products against their documentation, and name the page in `sources`.
4. **Decide.** Add or update proposals in `data/feedback/proposals.json`. Each has a decision (done, accepted, proposed, question, declined) and a reason; a done one names its version. Which points led to it is worked out, not written.
5. **Ask.** Anything only the reviewer can answer goes in `questions`.
6. `python3 admin/build/gate.py --build`, then release as usual.

Nothing a customer sends is published without their yes, and no contact details ever are: a test fails on an email address in `data/feedback/` other than ours.

## A synthetic study

Follow newsroom.sgit.ai's method, [How to run synthetic users](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/how-to-run-synthetic-users.html), as adapted in `data/feedback/synthetic/protocol.json`:

1. **Before any run:** the invented users in `personas.json` (a situation and a question, never a real person) and what each is expected to do in `journeys.json`.
2. **Freeze the site:** a local copy of the version under study, checked against the live site.
3. **Run:** one agent per invented user, each driving the browser only through `feedback/synthetic/tools/step.mjs`, which keeps one browser open for the run, reaches only the local copy and the two pinned APIs, and writes `_capture.json`. At most 14 actions, then the ten interview questions, a rating and three to six findings, in `run.json`.
4. **Check every finding** in `checks.json` against the capture, the screenshots, the site's files and outside documentation: confirmed, partly, artefact, or not confirmed. Keep every finding whatever its verdict.
5. **Decide,** as for a review: each finding leads to proposals in the register.
6. **Run the same users again** after the changes they led to, and compare.

The study pages say on every page that the users are invented and that this is not user research.


==============================================================================
source: /docs/ops/needs.md
==============================================================================

# What only a human can do

*customers.riskmandate.ai · operations · maintained by the build session · last updated at v0.2.2 (2026-10-21) · CC BY 4.0*

Everything on this list blocks a step of the brief or of the repository rules and cannot be done from inside the repository. Each item says who, what, exactly, and which step waits on it. Items are moved to *Done* when done, dated, and anything that turned out differently from the brief is recorded in [BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md](../brief/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md).

## Blocking the first release being live

1. **DNS (the lead).** `customers.riskmandate.ai CNAME risk-mandate.github.io` at the registrar for riskmandate.ai. The lead said on 2026-10-20 that this is being done now; by 20:55 UTC the host answered from GitHub Pages with a 404, which is the record in place and no site deployed yet.
2. **GitHub Pages (the lead, as an owner of Risk-Mandate).** On the repository `Risk-Mandate/Risk-Mandate-AI__Website__Customers`: Settings, Pages, source "GitHub Actions"; custom domain `customers.riskmandate.ai`; enforce HTTPS once the certificate is issued. The deploy job asks Pages to enable itself (`enablement: true`), but the custom domain and HTTPS are settings the token cannot set.
3. **Re-run `verify-live` (the lead).** The v0.1.0 run's last job polls the host for ten minutes and fails if the record is not there yet. When 1 and 2 are done, re-run the workflow from the Actions tab, or push the next release; the record in `data/versions.json` is filled at the next release.
4. **The Pages environment (the lead).** If the `github-pages` environment restricts deploy branches, add `dev`. The sibling sites hit this once.

## Blocking real money (the top-up)

5. **A payment link (the lead).** The meter charges on this site from v0.2.1, with £50.00 of credit to start. A top-up moves no money until there is a payment link: create one (a Stripe Payment Link, as the newsroom has), set its return address to `https://customers.riskmandate.ai/account/topped-up.html?session_id={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}`, and put it in `data/meter.json` as `config.topup.link` with the credit it buys as `config.topup.amount`. The meter's security model says what the return page does and does not check.
6. **The prices (the lead, with the batch).** The table in `data/meter.json` is a starting point: 1p for the home page, 2p a page, 10p a storyboard, 50p a behaviour policy, £1.00 the starter pack. Change it as the batch says what pages are worth.
6a. **The meter on the API (the newsroom's agent).** newsroom.sgit.ai runs SG Meter v1.5.0 from its own copy, which charges by the share of a page read; api.newsroom.sgit.ai's newest release, v0.2.5, has v1.4.1. When a release with v1.5.0 is published, this site moves to it by changing `data/meter.json` and the pinned manifest in `admin/build/pins/`.

## Blocking the next batch's form

7. **The form on this site (the lead, then the build session).** The riskmandate.ai contact form encrypts to the site agent's key and posts to the `site` lane of its comms vault. The same form on this site needs: the lead's yes; the lane's endpoint and token (public on purpose on riskmandate.ai) referenced, never copied into a new file; a content security policy change for `connect-src` and `form-action`; and a round trip proved. Until then the route is email or the riskmandate.ai form.

## The customer records

8. **The private list (the lead).** One file, held by the lead, never committed and never in a vault with a public read key: for each customer, the handle used on the site, the real name and how to reach them, the agent they named, the starting credit, and the private notes from the follow-ups. The public record in `data/customers.json` is the summary and carries none of it.
9. **The consultants and the colleagues (the lead).** The brief's other two groups are not listed yet. Each is added as a record when they start, by a handle they agreed to, by a release.
10. **The ten agents (the lead, with the wired-in agent).** A list of the agents the lead runs, one line each, with the published shape each is nearest to; two have behaviour policies today on riskmandate.ai/team/. This is step S1 of the record *the-agents*.

## Waiting on the feedback register

12a. **Three answers (the lead).** On [the reviews](../../feedback/reviews/index.md#questions): Q1, what "including the history" means in R001; Q2, whether the first try should show the line failing; Q3, what joining the first batch commits a company to. The guided path (P1, P2) is held for the further memos R001 announced, and for Q1.
12b. **Fail closed or open (the lead).** P18: whether the guard hook, RM-R0015, ships with `"onFailure": "block"`, which stops every action it watches when the hook cannot run, and needs Claude Code v2.1.295 or later.

## The estate's asks

11. **The honest column (the lead).** Add this site's row to the honest column on nfrs.sgit.ai. The row, as at v0.1.1: version control, met (one version, tagged, release history); reliability, partly (the gate and verify-live; no uptime record); resilience, not met (no backup beyond the repository and Pages); security, partly (the leak tripwire, a strict content security policy, no credentials in the tree; no branch protection yet); backups, not met; consistency, met (every number generated); explainability, met (the brief, the corrections, reality); documentation, met (twins, llms.txt, the ops notes).
12. **Branch protection (an owner of Risk-Mandate).** `dev` and `main` with `validate` as the required status check; no force pushes; the organisation's 2FA rule.

## Not yet needed

- A reviewer other than the lead for the follow-up messages: the lead sends them for the first batch.
- A comms identity of this site's own: it delegates to agent@riskmandate.ai, and `.well-known/sgit-agents.json` says so.

# How a release works

*customers.riskmandate.ai · operations · written at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20), the numbering changed at v0.2.1 (2026-10-21) · CC BY 4.0*

Every push to `dev` is a release. There is no build step at deploy time: the committed tree is the deployed tree, and seven small generators keep the parts that must agree in agreement. One pipeline validates, tags, deploys and then checks that the live site is serving what was pushed.

## The version

- The version lives in one file, `admin/build/version.txt`, as `X.Y.Z` with no `v`.
- Every push to `dev` moves the third number: `0.2.0`, `0.2.1`, `0.2.2`, `0.2.3`. The lead decided this on 21 October 2026, the way riskmandate.ai numbers its releases. The second number moves only when the lead says the site has become a different thing; the first is the lead's. `tag_release.py` accepts a patch, a minor or a major `.0.0`, so the gate does not change with the convention.
- The release commit's subject is `site vX.Y.Z : <what>`, with the same version. CI anchors on the newest commit whose subject has that shape, not on HEAD, because a merge commit may sit on top.
- `data/versions.json` gets a new first row: version, date, title, notes. The title is the `<what>` of the subject. The note says what changed and why, in words a reader can act on.
- The version is repeated by the generators into every page badge, every markdown twin, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, `sitemap.xml` and the release table. Check 1 of the gate fails on any disagreement.

## The steps, locally

```
# 1. edit content; edit data/customers.json, data/reality.json as the facts change
python3 admin/build/release.py --version X.Y.Z --kind feature --title "<what>" --notes "<why>"
#    which does: bump version.txt and versions.json; gate.py --build; commit "site vX.Y.Z : <what>"; push dev; verify live
# or by hand:
python3 admin/build/gate.py --build      # regenerate everything, then run the whole gate
git add -A
git commit -m "site vX.Y.Z : <what>"
git push -u origin dev                   # or open a pull request to dev from claude/<description>-<session-id>
```

`gate.py --build` runs the generators in order (customers, reality, docs, the review tools, chrome, versions, twins, llms), then runs them again with `--check`, then `node admin/build/validate.js`, then `python3 -m pytest tests/build/ -q`, then `node --test tests/unit/**/*.test.js`. `gate.py` without `--build` runs the same list in check mode only, which is exactly what CI does.

## The steps, in CI (`.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml`)

| Job | When | Does | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `validate` | every push to `dev` or `main`, every pull request to either, manual dispatch | `python3 admin/build/gate.py` | nothing is tagged or deployed |
| `tag-release` | push to `dev` only | `admin/build/tag_release.py`: version.txt equals the newest `site vX.Y.Z` subject; the version is the next minor, a patch or a major `.0.0` after the newest tag; backfills missing historical tags; pushes `refs/tags/vX.Y.Z` | no deploy |
| `deploy` | any push or dispatch, never a pull request | `admin/build/assemble_site.py` copies the tree minus `.git`, `.github`, `tests/unit`, `node_modules` into `_site/`; upload and deploy to GitHub Pages | the previous version stays live |
| `verify-live` | after deploy | `admin/build/verify_live.py` polls `https://customers.riskmandate.ai/admin/build/version.txt` and the home page badge with a cache-buster until both equal the version, for up to ten minutes | the run is red; the site may be stale |

A push to `main` deploys without tagging: `main` is promoted from `dev` and is the fallback. Both branches deploy to the one Pages site of this repository, so whichever pushed last is what the host serves; `main` is promoted only to a version `dev` already released.

## Green does not mean live

A sibling site once pushed two releases that reported success and never reached anyone, because the Pages deploy job died downloading its own action. The `verify-live` job exists for that reason: the release is not done until the origin answers with the new version. When `verify-live` is red and `deploy` is green, the usual causes are the domain not yet pointing at Pages (see [needs.md](needs.md)), Pages not yet enabled for the repository with the custom domain, or a transient `429` on an action download, which a re-run fixes. The first release of this site, v0.1.0, was pushed before the DNS record existed, so its `verify-live` is expected red until the lead's step is done; the re-run is the lead's.

## The eight checks of the gate

See `/admin/` on the site or the header of `admin/build/validate.js`. The rule for the leak tripwire is worth repeating: the fix for a trip is always a redaction, never a wider pattern. The rule for the house words is riskmandate.ai's: the verbatim documents are exempt and nothing else is. From v0.2.2 that includes the words of a reviewer or an invented user, which are kept as given: the memos in `data/feedback/memos/`, the runs in `data/feedback/synthetic/runs/`, a `"quote"` in a review's record, and any element marked `class="verbatim"`. Our own words around them are checked as usual.

## Backfilling tags

`tag_release.py` tags every historical release commit that has no tag, oldest first, then pushes all the new tags. A tag that already points at its release commit is left alone. A tag that points elsewhere fails the job: tags are never moved.

# The themes: six, one attribute, and how to add a seventh

*customers.riskmandate.ai · operations · written at v0.2.0 (2026-10-21) · CC BY 4.0*

The site has six themes, picked from the pill in the header and kept in the reader's browser. RiskMandate is the default and the first: riskmandate.ai's look, paper and green. Canvas is its dark variant, riskmandate.ai's dark hero band used as the whole page. The other four are newsroom.sgit.ai's themes, from its v0.12.12 of 13 October 2026, with the newsroom's values mapped onto this site's tokens.

| Theme | Mode | What it is | From |
|---|---|---|---|
| RiskMandate | light | paper and green, the default | riskmandate.ai |
| Canvas | dark | dark, green | riskmandate.ai's dark hero, as a whole page |
| Night | dark | dark, teal | newsroom.sgit.ai Night |
| Ember | dark | dark, amber | newsroom.sgit.ai Ember |
| Paper | light | warm cream, terracotta | newsroom.sgit.ai Paper |
| Blueprint | light | white, electric blue | newsroom.sgit.ai Blueprint |

## How it works

- **One attribute.** `assets/theme.js` sets `data-theme` on the html element before the first paint: it is a classic script in the head, loaded before the stylesheets, so the page never flashes the default first.
- **The reader's word is kept.** The stored choice comes first. With nothing stored, a system set to dark opens in Canvas and anything else in RiskMandate; the first choice in the picker ends that. The choice is one key in local storage, `riskmandate.customers.theme`, and never leaves the device. Print is the default theme on white, whatever the reader reads in.
- **Every colour is a token.** `assets/themes.css` is the only file on the site that writes a colour. It has one block per theme and every block defines every token. `assets/site.css` reads the tokens and writes no colour of its own.
- **The picker is drawn by the build.** `admin/build/chrome.py` writes the list from `data/themes.json` into every page's header; `theme.js` wires it and marks the current entry. Without JavaScript there is no choice and the page is the default.

## What the gate checks

`tests/build/test_themes.py` fails the build when any of these stop being true:

1. `data/themes.json`, `theme.js` and `themes.css` name the same themes, in the same order, with the default first and the same storage key.
2. Every theme block defines exactly the tokens the default defines; no theme falls through to another's colour.
3. No colour is written in `site.css`, the scripts or any page.
4. Each swatch in the picker is its theme's own `--rm-swatch`.
5. Each theme's `color-scheme` matches its mode, so the browser's own controls and scrollbars follow it.
6. In every theme, the pairs a reader reads hold their contrast: text, muted text, links and button ink at 4.5:1; labels, the hero's accent words and the step states at the levels their size allows.

The last check found one thing on the first run. riskmandate.ai's green, `#1A7F5A`, is 4.24:1 on its own alternate band, under the 4.5:1 a link needs. The accent here is `#187A56`, one shade darker and 4.53:1 there; the swatch and the shipped chip keep the brand green.

## Adding a theme

1. Add a row to `data/themes.json`: an id of lower-case letters, a name, a mode, a note of three or four words, and where it came from.
2. Add the id and name to `THEMES` in `assets/theme.js`, in the same position.
3. Copy the default block in `assets/themes.css`, rename it `:root[data-theme="<id>"]`, and give every token a value; add the `.sw-<id>` swatch.
4. Run `python3 admin/build/gate.py --build`. The contrast check names each pair that falls short; fix the value, not the threshold.

# The team

*customers.riskmandate.ai · who does what, as files · written at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · in the shape of the sgit.ai team section and the riskmandate.ai team page · CC BY 4.0*

Three roles fill every seat at this stage, held by one person and one agent. Each role is one file with the rules it enforces and the mistake behind each rule, so that a new agent can read this page and one role and begin. The board of work is [board.md](board.md), the work as files with a status line each, and [needs.md](../docs/ops/needs.md), the asks back to the person. Neither lives in a vault yet; if the board outgrows a file, it moves to a vault of its own and this page says where.

| Role | Held by | Decides |
|---|---|---|
| [Project lead](roles/project-lead.md) | Dinis Cruz | What ships next, what the brief means where it is ambiguous, who is in the batch and under what handle, the credit, everything that needs a human account (DNS, Pages, the meter, the list) |
| [Build agent](roles/build-agent.md) | A Claude Code session, one at a time | Everything else, within the rules its role file lists, recording each departure from the brief in the corrections file |
| [Customer follow-up](roles/customer-follow-up.md) | The lead, for the first batch; an agent drafts | The daily contact with each customer, the three questions, and what is recorded on the customer page |

The agents that make riskmandate.ai have behaviour policies of their own on [its team page](https://riskmandate.ai/team/); this site's build agent is a Claude Code session of the same kind and will get one as part of the record *the-agents* in the batch. Other teams review the work and the review is published with the reply; the first review this site expects is the sgit.ai site team's, against its repository rules.

# Role: build agent

*customers.riskmandate.ai · the Claude Code session · written at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · CC BY 4.0*

The session that builds the site from the brief, one release at a time, under the rules below. It never pushes a release that fails the gate, never writes a secret or a contact detail into the tree, and never describes a thing in the present tense before `data/reality.json` says shipped.

## Rules this role enforces, and the mistake behind each

| Rule | The mistake it came from |
|---|---|
| Run `python3 admin/build/gate.py --build` before every commit; CI runs the same command. | A sibling site shipped two releases that reported success and never reached anyone; the gate and verify-live exist for that reason. |
| Every number on a page is generated from a file or dated with the file it came from. | nfrs.sgit.ai's rule: an index maintained by hand becomes a lie on a schedule. The counts, the batch table and reality are written by scripts. |
| Never "ADP", never "the policy" alone, no score on a behaviour policy, "steps" not "rungs", British English. | riskmandate.ai's rules, each with a reason on its own CLAUDE.md; the gate enforces them here, and the verbatim brief and memo are exempt. |
| No contact details in any file; the gate fails on anything contact-shaped in the customer records. | The brief's "no customer is named"; the repository is public. |
| When the brief is wrong, record it in BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md and carry on; never edit the brief or the memo. | The brief is the one that was accepted; the memo is the one that was said. |
| When something needs a human, write exactly what, as a command, in needs.md, and continue with what does not depend on it. | A step that lives in a chat does not get done. |
| The fix for a tripwire hit is a redaction, never a wider pattern. | A wider pattern hides the next real key. |
| No em-dashes in prose the session writes; the gate says so as an advisory. | The house prose rule; the verbatim documents are exempt. |
| A release is `site vX.Y.Z : what`, the version bumped, the note saying what changed and why. | "UI improvements" tells a reader nothing; the release history is the repository's memory. |

## Starting prompt

"Read README.md, docs/ops/release.md, docs/brief/BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md and team/board.md. Continue from the first open row on the board that does not wait on the lead. Every release is `site vX.Y.Z : what` with the third number moved by one (v0.2.1, then v0.2.2) and a `Kind:` trailer."

# Role: customer follow-up

*customers.riskmandate.ai · held by the lead for the first batch; an agent drafts · written at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · CC BY 4.0*

The daily contact with each customer. Asks three things, as often as daily if that helps: what they did, what got in the way, what is next. Records the answers on the customer page in summary and keeps the rest with the lead. The pattern is the newsroom's: an agent drafts, a person reads and sends, and nothing goes out that a person has not seen.

## Rules this role enforces, and the mistake behind each

| Rule | The mistake it came from |
|---|---|
| Three questions, a line each is plenty; "nothing, I was busy" is a fine answer and goes in the log. | A follow-up that reads as a form gets no reply; Paul Graham's attentiveness is a person asking, not a survey. |
| The log on the customer page is the summary; names of systems, the contents of a grant or a mandate, and anything the customer did not want public stay with the lead. | The brief: nothing is published without their yes, and the default is no. |
| The second answer, what got in the way, is read against the three questions on the learning page, and a pattern across customers becomes a finding with its count. | A finding typed before it was counted is a guess; the learning page's table starts empty on purpose. |
| A customer who has not replied is asked again, not marked. | A status that says "stalled" is a judgement; the log records dates and the ladder records steps. |
| The follow-up names the step the customer is on and links their page, so they can see what the site says about them. | A page about a person that the person has not seen is a page they cannot correct. |

## The message

The template is on [the follow-up page](../../follow-up/index.md). An agent fills `{first name}`, `{step}` and `{id}` from the private list and the customer record; a person sends it from agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Starting prompt

"For each customer in data/customers.json whose status is not example, draft today's follow-up from the template, with the step they are on and the link to their page, and put the drafts where the lead reads them. Do not send."

source: /team/roles/project-lead.md
==============================================================================

# Role: project lead

*customers.riskmandate.ai · Dinis Cruz · written at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · CC BY 4.0*

The person. Speaks or writes the brief; an agent drafts; the person accepts. Decides who is in the batch and under what handle, what the credit is, what the brief means where it is ambiguous, and everything that needs a human account.

## Rules this role enforces, and the mistake behind each

| Rule | The mistake it came from |
|---|---|
| A brief is the person's words, in either hand, and is published in full before the work starts. | A site built from a conversation nobody can read cannot be checked against anything but itself; the repository rules say so and the newsroom's briefs are the pattern. |
| Nobody is listed as a customer without their yes, and the default is no. | The brief's own rule, "no customer is named"; the memo named the first users, and C2 in the corrections says how that was reconciled. |
| A customer's private details never enter the repository; the lead holds them. | The repository is public and every file in it is deployed; a leak is an incident, not a typo. |
| Every ask that needs a human is written as a command in needs.md, and the lead does it or says why not. | The sibling sites' DNS and Pages steps sat undone because they were in a chat, not on a page. |
| The lead reads the correction above the mistake, never edits the brief to match. | A corrected brief would no longer be the one that was accepted. |

## Starting prompt

"Read the start-here page as a customer would and say where it is hard to understand. Then read needs.md and do the first open item or say why not."

# Corrections to the review brief, for this repository

*customers.riskmandate.ai · started at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · CC BY 4.0*

The review brief is [Code review graphs in the repository](https://sgit.ai/docs/briefs/code-review-graphs-in-the-repository.html), on sgit.ai. Where this repository does not follow it, the entry is here, dated, with the reason.

## R1. Only the intent half exists at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20)

The brief asks a new repository to build the whole folder before its first source file. This repository built the intent half (stories, rules, examples, anchored to the brief and the memo), a validator and a static rendering, and shipped the site. The derived half, the join, the change files, the web-component navigator and `self/` are proposed, recorded in `data/reality.json` as *site.review-derived*. Reason: the site had to exist on the day the brief was accepted; a review folder for a site that does not exist reviews nothing. The next change starts the derived half, delta first.

## R2. The brief's headings are not numbered (2026-10-20)

The review brief's `sections.json` keys sections by number. The newsroom article that is this site's brief has prose headings with no numbers, so `tools/sections.py` keys them by the heading's slug, which is also the anchor on the rendered page. The memo document is anchored the same way, and both are in one `sections.json` under `docs`.

## R3. The navigator is a page, not components (2026-10-20)

The brief asks for a navigator built as web components in the coding.sgit.ai shape. `review/index.html` is a static page rendered by `tools/render.py`, with the same links a navigator would have (every node to its section of the brief and to the page it lands on), and no script. The components come with the derived half.

source: /review/README.md

# review/: the brief as intent, and what is not derived yet

*customers.riskmandate.ai · written at v0.1.0 (2026-10-20) · CC BY 4.0*

The sgit.ai repository rules ask every repository to carry a review folder from its first commit, in the shape of [Code review graphs in the repository](https://sgit.ai/docs/briefs/code-review-graphs-in-the-repository.html): the intent written top down from the brief, the code derived bottom up from the syntax tree by parsers, the join between the two with a coverage figure, every commit read upwards, a navigator built as web components, and `self/` for the tools. This folder has the first of those and says so.

## What is here

- `intent/stories.json`: the brief and the memo as stories, rules and examples, written by the build session on 2026-10-20, each node carrying the document and the heading it came from. Not yet accepted by a person; the lead accepts by a release that sets `accepted_by`.
- `intent/sections.json`: every heading of the brief and the memo with the anchor the rendered page gives it, generated by `tools/sections.py`, so every source resolves to a place a reader can click.
- `tools/validate_review.py`: the shape checks; it runs in the gate. `tools/render.py` renders the intent into [the review page](index.html), static HTML with no script.
- [BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md](BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md): where the review brief was not followed, and why.

## What is not here

The derived half: `graph/`, `join/`, `changes/`, `streams/`, `checks/`, the navigator as web components, and `self/`. The reality file carries it as *site.review-derived*, proposed. The plan is the repository rules' own: from the next change, delta first, letting the graph grow along the paths people walk.

## Regenerate and check

```
python3 review/tools/sections.py             # the headings of the brief and the memo, with anchors
python3 review/tools/validate_review.py      # every source resolves; every surface is a page; ids unique
python3 review/tools/render.py               # the review page
```
